sectionTitles: Building with tides and fish in mind

passages.text: Tla’amin people live on the northern Sunshine Coast of British Columbia, with longstanding relationships across its lands and waters. The name of the main community, t̓išosəm, recalls waters whitened by herring spawn. Marine knowledge, family responsibilities and self-government remain central to the Nation’s life.

passages.title: Building with tides and fish in mind
passages.text: Stone fish traps on the Sliammon shoreline include semicircular enclosures. In Desolation Sound, some walls enhanced natural pools, holding fish as the tide receded. These surviving structures demonstrate deliberate modification of the shore around local water movement.

passages.title: Building with tides and fish in mind
passages.text: Other Desolation Sound traps used wooden stakes that supported barriers. Water preserved lower portions of the stakes after exposed wood disappeared. Archaeologists must reconstruct the working installation from these incomplete remains rather than treating what survives as its original height.

passages.title: Building with tides and fish in mind
passages.text: Trap designs could also combine stone or wooden guiding lines with removable woven baskets. Different structures served different settings and catches. Their variety reflects knowledge of fish movement as well as skill in construction.

passages.title: Harvest and household food
passages.text: Herring rakes were swept through schools of fish. Their teeth could be made from sharpened wood or bone, with iron nails used in more recent versions. The changing materials show an established harvesting method adapting to new supplies.

passages.title: Harvest and household food
passages.text: Fresh herring could be boiled or roasted, while smoking and sun-drying made it possible to store the catch. Preservation extended the value of a seasonal abundance beyond the day of fishing.

passages.title: Harvest and household food
passages.text: For roe collection, hemlock or cedar boughs were placed in the water during spawning. The eggs could be eaten fresh or dried. This used the fish’s spawning behaviour to obtain food without relying on the same tools as the fish harvest.

passages.title: Harvest and household food
passages.text: A Tla’amin-area research project combined trap mapping and archaeological sampling with community knowledge. Its researchers described studying old herring bones and their DNA to investigate abundance and diversity. Those methods ask about past fisheries; they do not by themselves establish the result.

passages.title: Knowledge, care and community
passages.text: The Nation describes kinship as a basis for rights, responsibilities and mutual support across villages. Elders transmit teachings through stories, instruction and example. Family relationships connect practical care with knowledge of territory.

passages.title: Knowledge, care and community
passages.text: Ancestral names are held by families and passed on with responsibilities. Naming and memorial gatherings affirm relationships and obligations. In the Nation’s account, ceremony is part of governance, rather than an activity detached from public life.

passages.title: Knowledge, care and community
passages.text: Tla’amin’s contemporary service model draws on making and caring for a baby basket. Preparation, weaving and maintenance provide ways to think about coordinated care and responsibility. Craft knowledge becomes a guide for designing present-day community services.

passages.title: Knowledge, care and community
passages.text: Language work includes workshops, recordings and resources for citizens living away from Tla’amin lands. Cultural staff also support heritage protection and repatriation inquiries. Keeping knowledge in circulation involves families, teachers, archives and community institutions.

passages.title: Knowledge, care and community
passages.text: On September 3, 2025, the Executive Council adopted a five-year strategy for ʔayʔaǰuθəm revitalisation. Its stated purpose is to strengthen the language’s presence in community life. Adopting a plan is a documented action, not proof that all its aims have been achieved.

Colonial dispossession and the removal of children disrupted Tla’amin life. The Nation continues to rebuild services, cultural transmission and relationships with its territory. Its treaty took effect in 2016, restoring self-government within a new relationship with Canada and British Columbia; Tla’amin history continues.

sectionTitles: Research and recovery on the rivers

passages.text: Cofán people live across the river and forest country of northeastern Ecuador and southern Colombia, where Amazonian lowlands approach the Andes. Their language is A’ingae. Hunting, fishing, forest knowledge and community leadership remain important, alongside changing forms of education, income and territorial protection.

passages.title: Forest materials and everyday skills
passages.text: A study published in 2010 documented necklaces, baskets, cordage, dyes and other crafts during visits to Sábalo from 2007 to 2009. Makers combined plant materials with animal-derived elements and some plastic beads. Forest knowledge supported both household work and the sale of crafts.

passages.title: Forest materials and everyday skills
passages.text: The same study identified seeds, leaves, fruits and fibres among the materials used in craftwork. Necklaces drew on especially varied forest resources. Producing them required recognizing suitable materials and turning them into objects with uses beyond the plant itself.

passages.title: Forest materials and everyday skills
passages.text: In the early 2000s, coastal Ecuadorian boat makers taught Cofán builders to make fibreglass canoes. The project adapted an established form of river transport while reducing the need to cut large canoe trees. Some trainees developed boat-building businesses.

passages.title: Forest materials and everyday skills
passages.text: A later canoe project experimented with batteries, charging stations and electric motors. Its aim is to reduce dependence on fossil fuel and provide quieter river travel. The published account describes work in use and development, with wider commercial expansion still a goal.

passages.title: Research and recovery on the rivers
passages.text: A turtle-recovery effort began in 1990 around the Aguarico and Zábalo rivers. Community members protected young turtles in pools before release, alongside restrictions on adult hunting and changes in egg collection. Recovery involved changing harvest practices as well as raising hatchlings.

passages.title: Research and recovery on the rivers
passages.text: Cofán researchers tested interviews, canoe-based turtle counts and surveys of nests on beaches. Comparing these methods made community observations available as a research record. The 2005 paper reported positive trends from two methods, without treating all observations as equally reliable measures.

passages.title: Research and recovery on the rivers
passages.text: A later study examined nesting records from 1994 to 2019. It found improving indicators for Podocnemis unifilis, but called for more work on age-specific population trends and the rarer P. expansa. Success with one species did not establish equal recovery for both.

passages.title: Work, learning and land care
passages.text: Early boundary patrols relied on families giving time away from food production and paid work. The later Park Guard programme paid people to monitor territory and maintain access points. Supporting the guards’ households was part of making territorial protection sustainable.

passages.title: Work, learning and land care
passages.text: Patrol groups brought people from different villages together, including older members who shared stories in forest camps. The programme’s account describes this as a setting for passing on historical and ecological knowledge while doing practical work.

passages.title: Work, learning and land care
passages.text: Dureno’s conservation efforts included community hunting and fishing rules and an area where hunting was excluded so wildlife could reproduce. Food security and forest protection were connected concerns in the Field Museum’s 2007 account.

passages.title: Work, learning and land care
passages.text: In Colombia, a participatory project worked with older Cofán women, healers, learners and families to document botanical knowledge. Interviews, visits to gardens and reserves, and plant illustrations contributed to a 2011 publication intended to help knowledge pass between generations.

passages.title: Work, learning and land care
passages.text: Cofán tourism programmes train guides to explain forest life, manage journeys and communicate with visitors. The Survival Fund describes this as teaching outsiders through ecological expertise. Guiding combines inherited knowledge with language learning and the practical work of hosting people.

Cofán communities continue in Ecuador and Colombia. Oil development, settlement and forest damage have restricted access to ancestral lands and resources. Community institutions, territorial protection and knowledge-sharing are responses to these pressures; they are part of a continuing history, not evidence of a people’s disappearance.

passages.text: W̱SÁNEĆ people describe themselves as Salt Water People. Their homeland includes the Saanich Peninsula and neighbouring islands and waters. Fishing places, winter villages, language and responsibilities to other living beings connect this history with continuing community life.

passages.title: Engineering in moving water
passages.text: Dave Elliott remembered helping prepare reef-net ropes, floats and stone anchors as a boy. He emphasised the knowledge of tides, wind and rope strength needed to keep equipment in place. A fishing installation depended on careful local judgement, not simply a net.

passages.title: Engineering in moving water
passages.text: Elliott explained that willow inner bark supplied strong twine for the reef net. The material’s preparation and strength mattered in fast-moving salt water. His account links plant knowledge on land with equipment used far from shore.

passages.title: Engineering in moving water
passages.text: The Council describes families as custodians of particular reef nets and harvesting locations. Fishing was therefore embedded in responsibilities toward places and marine life, as well as in the work of catching and sharing food.

passages.title: Engineering in moving water
passages.text: Youth-project coordinator Edna Ellsworth explains that the net guides salmon upward and includes an opening through which some can escape. The design combines capture with provision for fish to continue their journey.

passages.title: Engineering in moving water
passages.text: In August 2025, the youth team adjusted weights and successfully positioned its net in the water. The team caught no fish on that outing. The documented achievement was learning how to deploy the equipment, rather than a demonstrated harvest.

passages.title: Gardening the shore
passages.text: Clam gardens use rock walls to retain sediment and create flatter intertidal habitat. Maintaining such a shore involves moving stones and tending the beach. These food-producing places show people actively shaping marine environments.

passages.title: Gardening the shore
passages.text: Recent restoration at Fulford Harbour and other sites brings together wall repair, sediment tending, youth education and laboratory testing of shellfish. Harvests that meet safety requirements are shared with community members, including Elders. This is continuing practical work, not only preservation of old structures.

passages.title: Seasonal knowledge and community
passages.text: The account of ĆENŦEḴI, the Sockeye Moon, connects salmon fishing with summer weather, bird calls and ripening strawberries and salmonberries. Its calendar guides related activities through the seasons; its moons do not correspond exactly to modern calendar months.

passages.title: Seasonal knowledge and community
passages.text: Catching salmon in the straits before they reached rivers supported exchange with inland peoples. The Council’s seasonal account links this timing to a trading advantage, showing how ecological knowledge shaped economic relationships.

passages.title: Seasonal knowledge and community
passages.text: The same account describes pausing fishing for a ceremony when the first sockeye was caught. Songs, prayer and a shared meal acknowledged the salmon. Food gathering and spiritual responsibilities belonged to a connected practice.

Colonial fishing restrictions and residential schooling disrupted harvesting and language transmission. W̱SÁNEĆ communities continue to assert responsibilities to their homeland and rebuild fisheries, teaching and ecological care. These are histories of continuing people, not a vanished civilisation.

sectionTitles: Canoes, carving and the transmission of skill
Keeping language and community knowledge accessible

passages.text: Tla-o-qui-aht homeland lies around Meares Island, Tofino and Long Beach on Vancouver Island’s west coast, extending inland beyond Sutton Pass. Fishing, carving, singing and dancing connect community life with this territory. Tla-o-qui-aht people continue to govern, teach and care for their lands and waters.

passages.title: Territory, stewardship and everyday work
passages.text: The Nation describes traditional place names as records of occupation and cultural use. Some protected places have particular conditions of access, guided by the Ha’wiih. Knowing the landscape includes understanding responsibilities toward places, beyond knowing how to reach them.

passages.title: Territory, stewardship and everyday work
passages.text: Ha’wiih, the hereditary chiefs, hold responsibilities for lands, resources and cultural activities. The Nation describes this leadership as a continuing part of its governance. Territorial care and cultural life are linked in these responsibilities.

passages.title: Territory, stewardship and everyday work
passages.text: Guardians restore river and salmon habitat, monitor activities, maintain trails and remove invasive plants and marine debris. The programme brings ecological knowledge into paid work and practical care of places also visited by tourists.

passages.title: Territory, stewardship and everyday work
passages.text: The Tribal Parks report describes salmon hatchery work involving Chinook and coho, as well as habitat restoration. Such projects link fisheries with care for waterways. The account documents activities; it does not establish a measured recovery of every fish population.

passages.title: Territory, stewardship and everyday work
passages.text: Other reported projects include maintaining the Big Tree Trail boardwalk, involving Junior Guardians and providing food hampers during the COVID period. Visitor infrastructure, youth learning and household support all form part of the programme’s community work.

passages.title: Canoes, carving and the transmission of skill
passages.text: Tutakwisnapšiƛ, Joe Martin, is a Tla-o-qui-aht Elder and master dugout-canoe carver. The Royal BC Museum describes his contribution to renewing canoe making in his own Nation and neighbouring communities. A working craft survives through skilled people who practise and share it.

passages.title: Canoes, carving and the transmission of skill
passages.text: Reflecting on museum collections, Martin described belongings removed during the suppression of potlatches and argued that some had been confiscated rather than freely collected. His account places the objects within histories of families, ceremony and colonial power.

passages.title: Canoes, carving and the transmission of skill
passages.text: Artist Joe David was born at Opitsaht and later studied and worked in art beyond his home community. His training included relationships with Bill Holm and Duane Pasco. The Museum of Anthropology held a solo exhibition of his work in 1978.

passages.title: Canoes, carving and the transmission of skill
passages.text: A small wooden mask by Joe David in the Metropolitan Museum is dated to 1981 to 1988. Painted surfaces and carved form are both part of the work. Its recorded maker and date show an individual artist working within a living artistic tradition.

passages.title: Canoes, carving and the transmission of skill
passages.text: Douglas David’s Chihaa mask, representing an eagle as a young boy, combines wood and paint with cedar bark, animal hair, abalone shell and leather. The Burke Museum’s catalogue records carving, painting and joining as parts of making this particular object.

passages.title: Keeping language and community knowledge accessible
passages.text: A 2023 language-technology job posting described transferring cassette tapes, VHS recordings and documents into digital formats. The work included organizing audio and video and recording information about each item. Careful archival work helps keep recordings of fluent Elders usable for later learning.

passages.title: Keeping language and community knowledge accessible
passages.text: The reconciliation process established in 2022 included elected and hereditary representatives, advisers and Elders. Its published approach brings proposals back to the community for discussion. Negotiation is connected to local priorities for services, well-being and future generations.

Tla-o-qui-aht continues as a living Nation. Its agreements with British Columbia and Canada establish processes for negotiating relationships and community needs. They should not be read as the end of its people, a surrender of its asserted inherent authority or a completed final settlement.

passages.text: A’uwẽ, often called Xavante, are a Jê-speaking people with communities in Mato Grosso, Brazil. Their communities share language, ceremonial life and forms of social organisation while retaining political autonomy. Histories of migration, outside contact and land loss differ between communities; they are not a single kingdom with one founding or fall date.

passages.title: Food, movement and learning
passages.text: In Sereburã’s recollections of childhood, families travelled through the landscape to hunt and gather. Young people learned by watching adults. Scouts also brought fresh maize from village gardens to people on trek, connecting cultivation with mobile food gathering.

passages.title: Food, movement and learning
passages.text: At Pimentel Barbosa and Etênhiritipá, Welch describes maize loaves, wild roots, macaúba and game as important ceremonial gifts. Producing and sharing food helped sustain obligations between people, even as purchased foods became more common in daily meals.

passages.title: Food, movement and learning
passages.text: Welch records growers experimenting with soils and fallow periods after larger gardens became necessary. Some women recalled selecting and exchanging maize kernels by colour to maintain preferred varieties. Their explanations of declining maize vigour were hypotheses rooted in observation, not a single experimentally established cause.

passages.title: Making useful objects
passages.text: Xavante bag baskets in the Museu Índia Vanuíre are woven from buriti palm fibre, with lids and carrying straps. The catalogue records vertical twisted weaving and different sizes made for personal use and sale. Construction joins plant knowledge with the needs of carrying and storing.

passages.title: Making useful objects
passages.text: The same museum’s Xavante sieve has an open woven surface reinforced by wooden rods and cotton bindings. Its catalogue identifies use in sifting maize, bean and sweet-manioc flour. The spacing of the weave makes a working surface for preparing food.

passages.title: Making useful objects
passages.text: A wooden mortar catalogued as made in 1988 survives in the Museu Nacional dos Povos Indígenas. It is hollowed from a wooden cylinder, with a shaped base. This particular utensil preserves evidence of woodworking for household processing.

passages.title: Making useful objects
passages.text: A 2021 gathering of Xavante women included collecting buriti leaves and making baquité baskets used in daily tasks and for carrying children. Making objects together provided a practical setting for transmitting skills across generations.

passages.title: Seeds, exchange and public voice
passages.text: At the 2017 Ripá seed fair, families exchanged maize, bean, gourd, cotton and tree seeds. They discussed the loss of locally maintained varieties when seed saving gave way to annual purchases. The fair connected cultivation with retaining control over planting material.

passages.title: Seeds, exchange and public voice
passages.text: Women collectors from Ripá prepared native Cerrado seeds for sale to restoration projects. Hunters shared information about where trees were fruiting, helping collectors plan their work. Different forms of landscape knowledge contributed to both income and restoration.

passages.title: Seeds, exchange and public voice
passages.text: Chief Carolina Rewaptu described family plots producing maize, rice, beans and squash. Participants linked food production with the space needed for hunting, gathering, fishing and cultivation. Seed exchange addressed a wider problem of restricted access to territory.

passages.title: Seeds, exchange and public voice
passages.text: Mário Juruna became Brazil’s first Indigenous federal deputy. The Chamber of Deputies preserves his April 19, 1983 speech. This record places a Xavante leader’s own public voice within the national parliamentary archive.

A’uwẽ communities continue to transmit language, organise ceremonies and defend their territories. Colonial expansion and state policies transformed their autonomy and livelihoods. Marãiwatsédé’s recovery in 2013 was one major community achievement, followed by the work of rebuilding life on damaged land; it was not the end of Xavante history.

sectionTitles: Buffalo and the work of restoration

passages.text: The Aaniiih, also known as Gros Ventre or White Clay People, are a Northern Plains people. At Fort Belknap in northern Montana, they share a government with the Nakoda. Buffalo, material skills, language and community institutions connect their history with continuing work to sustain culture and livelihoods.

passages.title: Food, shelter and skilled making
passages.text: The community’s history describes buffalo as a source of food, clothing and tipi coverings. Following herds required knowledge of animal movement and the skills to preserve meat and work hides for several different purposes.

passages.title: Food, shelter and skilled making
passages.text: In testimony gathered in 1901, women described slicing meat thinly and drying it on racks. Dried meat could be stored in rawhide containers or pounded with berries. Preservation supported households beyond the immediate hunt.

passages.title: Food, shelter and skilled making
passages.text: Tent making could be cooperative: a woman with enough prepared hides invited skilled makers to a feast. An expert fitted the pieces before others sewed them together, combining hospitality with specialised work.

passages.title: Food, shelter and skilled making
passages.text: Kroeber described a child’s robe, museum number 50-1751, decorated with coloured quillwork, tin and dyed horsehair pendants. The object records several materials and techniques used together in clothing.

passages.title: Food, shelter and skilled making
passages.text: A soft-hide bag, museum number 50-1738, appears in the same report. Such bags carried clothing and small household articles, with quillwork and beadwork adding decoration to a practical container.

passages.title: Knowledge in community institutions
passages.text: Aaniiih Nakoda College was designed to make further education available near home and reflect the lifeways of both Nations. Its programmes connect cultural study with fields such as ecology, nursing, computing and trades. The name adopted in 2011 explicitly recognises both peoples.

passages.title: Knowledge in community institutions
passages.text: In 2014, educator Clarena Brockie described White Clay Immersion School’s use of community projects, field learning and teaching between generations. Language was the means of learning across subjects, giving children sustained opportunities to use it.

passages.title: Knowledge in community institutions
passages.text: A reference grammar published in 2024 grew from work by Andrew Cowell, Terry Brockie and tribal members to retranscribe archival language records. It explains both earlier and modern forms, supporting community decisions about what to teach and how.

passages.title: Knowledge in community institutions
passages.text: The grammar also treats place names, personal names, greetings and traditional narrative. Preserving language involves how people address one another and describe their world, alongside its sounds and word structures.

passages.title: Buffalo and the work of restoration
passages.text: In August 2013, Yellowstone-origin bison arrived from Fort Peck to establish a new cultural herd at Fort Belknap. The project linked conservation with food and ceremonial uses. This was a specific restoration programme within an already living community.

passages.title: Buffalo and the work of restoration
passages.text: A project funded in 2024 planned wildlife-friendly fencing and a livestock water system to bring more pasture into the buffalo grazing system. Managing a herd also involves water, land access, infrastructure and consultation about cultural resources.

Reservation confinement and assimilation policies reduced Aaniiih autonomy and disrupted language transmission. Aaniiih people continue, sharing the Fort Belknap government with Nakoda neighbours and building institutions for education and cultural renewal. The decline of fluent speakers did not mean the disappearance of the people or an end to language learning.

sectionTitles: Markets and the people who made cloth

passages.text: The Abdelwadids, also called Zayyanids, made Tlemcen the capital of a kingdom in the central Maghreb. Emerging from Zenata leadership as Almohad power weakened, they supported a city connected to trans-Saharan and Mediterranean trade.

passages.title: Markets and the people who made cloth
passages.text: A marble tablet from Tlemcen’s bazaar carries an inscription dating it to 1328 and identifying it as a cubit measure. Its ruled line is divided into four parts. The object made a common unit of length physically available in a place of commerce.

passages.title: Markets and the people who made cloth
passages.text: The catalogue reports that this tablet was found set into the bazaar wall. It is evidence for a local measurement standard, not proof that the ruler invented the cubit or that every sale followed the rule without dispute.

passages.title: Markets and the people who made cloth
passages.text: Textile production employed both men and women in Zayyanid Tlemcen. A study of the industry links its growth to available raw materials, trading connections and expertise arriving from al-Andalus. Making cloth connected household livelihoods with the city’s wider economy.

passages.title: Markets and the people who made cloth
passages.text: The same study describes demand from different social groups, including elite customers seeking refined fabrics. Quality and finish mattered to makers as well as access to materials. The surviving record does not justify treating every textile worker as prosperous.

passages.title: Architecture and learning
passages.text: An inscription dates the Sidi Bel-Hasan mosque to 1296. Onyx columns support horseshoe arches dividing the prayer hall into three aisles, while cedar roof structures carried tile coverings. A relatively small building brought together stoneworking, carpentry and brick construction.

passages.title: Architecture and learning
passages.text: Traces of coloured paint survive on the mosque’s plaster decoration. Its prayer niche combines inscriptions and floral ornament with a muqarnas dome, formed from small projecting cells. Later alterations mean that the building’s present appearance is not wholly medieval.

passages.title: Architecture and learning
passages.text: At the royal Mechouar, Abu Hammu Musa I completed a mosque in 1317 to 1318. The square minaret preserves panels of small columns and arches against tiled mosaics. Its decoration records skilled work within the court’s architectural setting.

passages.title: Architecture and learning
passages.text: Tlemcen’s teaching took place in mosques and madrasas, with study of Islamic law, Qur’anic interpretation, hadith and Sufism. Rulers’ support helped attract teachers and students from other regions, connecting the city with a wider scholarly world.

passages.title: Architecture and learning
passages.text: The Mechouar began as Yaghmurasan’s royal seat in the thirteenth century and was enlarged by successors. Modern conservation has also shaped it: a project sheet records major work on tile and plaster decoration between 2008 and 2012. Present surfaces need to be read alongside that restoration history.

passages.title: Coins and contested sovereignty
passages.text: Two gold dinars in the Bibliothèque nationale de France, catalogued as Lavoix 986 and 987, name Tlemcen and two rulers. Mohamed Elhadri argues that they belong to sixteenth-century Zayyanids acknowledging the Ottoman sultan Süleyman, rather than an earlier Marinid and Nasrid alliance.

passages.title: Coins and contested sovereignty
passages.text: Elhadri tests that attribution against the names, titles and mint formulas on the coins and the chronology of political alliances. The case shows why a familiar royal name alone may misdate an object, especially when local monetary forms survive changes of overlord.

passages.title: Coins and contested sovereignty
passages.text: In 1517, one Tlemcen faction invited Aruj from Algiers while another backed the Zayyanid ruler with Spanish help. Aruj was killed after fleeing in 1518. Local choices and rivalries were central to this struggle, alongside the ambitions of larger powers.

Ottoman expansion ended Zayyanid rule around the middle of the sixteenth century. Sources date the final transition differently; approximately 1554 is a conventional endpoint. The royal citadel passed into Ottoman use, while Tlemcen and its inhabitants continued beyond the dynasty.

sectionTitles: Making containers, clothing and useful tools

passages.text: The Abipones were peoples of the Chaco, especially its southern frontier, organised through local groups and shifting alliances rather than one central kingdom. Their history combines hunting, gathering, skilled making and extensive exchange. Horses, iron tools, colonial missions and provincial governments changed that world without producing one universal date of conquest.

passages.title: Food work and movement
passages.text: Hunting, fishing and gathering supported households, with fruit, roots and honey alongside meat. Lucaioli cautions that surviving documents cannot establish the exact balance of these foods before European contact. Later increases in cattle and the use of horses changed available choices.

passages.title: Food work and movement
passages.text: One account describes families drying animals’ skins near a lake while collecting honey in nearby woods. Lucaioli uses this example to show that expeditions could combine several tasks and include whole families, complicating a simple picture of men hunting alone.

passages.title: Making containers, clothing and useful tools
passages.text: Dobrizhoffer described Abipón women shaping clay pots and pitchers by hand. Vitar examines this testimony as evidence of skilled work that colonial writers often undervalued. It is a written description of production, not an identification of a particular excavated vessel.

passages.title: Making containers, clothing and useful tools
passages.text: Women prepared skins for clothing and worked wool into dyed textiles. The equipment described for Abipón weaving included portable cane and wooden pieces that could be carried on horseback. Mobility therefore did not prevent technically demanding manufacture.

passages.title: Making containers, clothing and useful tools
passages.text: Mission authorities used existing textile skills to demand regular labour and to supply clothing. Vitar shows how colonial praise for women’s industry also served attempts to control their time. The adoption of wool and cotton did not mean that missionaries had invented weaving for them.

passages.title: Exchange and the mission economy
passages.text: Horses enabled longer journeys and the transport of more goods. Cattle and horses also became exchange goods for salt, tools, weapons, clothing and yerba. Lucaioli and Nesis describe these connections as growing economic interdependence between Indigenous groups and colonial society.

passages.title: Exchange and the mission economy
passages.text: The researchers distinguish community cattle used for food, herds held by influential leaders and animals acquired for trade. These categories matter because a mission’s herd was not simply a measure of every resident’s personal wealth. Different animals supported different social obligations.

passages.title: Exchange and the mission economy
passages.text: Concepción’s buildings included a chapel and missionaries’ rooms, but also carpentry and blacksmithing workshops and mills. The local museum’s account makes clear that the settlement involved practical production as well as religious instruction.

passages.title: Exchange and the mission economy
passages.text: The same account records repeated relocation of Concepción in response to environmental difficulties and conflict. Its changing sites illustrate why a mission’s name should not be treated as one permanently occupied town with fixed borders.

passages.title: Reading a contested historical record
passages.text: Letters and inventories can expose the practical arrangements behind a mission. A 1748 San Jerónimo founding record listed cattle, sheep, carts, oxen, axes and a portable altar, placing food, transport and tools alongside worship in plans for the settlement.

passages.title: Reading a contested historical record
passages.text: Green’s study uses correspondence, military reports and financial records to reassess the 1836 to 1838 conflict. He finds that settlement at El Sauce did not imply unconditional submission: groups retained distinct leaders and could leave, negotiate or resist.

Missions, warfare, displacement and incorporation into provincial society transformed Abipón communities unevenly. The nineteenth-century record shows both resistance and assimilation, rather than a single surrender by a unified state. Destruction of one settlement cannot establish that every Abipón person or descendant disappeared.

sectionTitles: Pottery and glass beads as evidence

passages.text: Abitibiwinni Aki is the ancestral territory of a living Anicinabe people whose history centres on Lake Abitibi and its connecting waterways. Families sustained themselves through fishing, hunting, trapping and gathering, returning to shared summer meeting places. Today the community at Pikogan maintains these relationships through land use, teaching and research.

passages.title: Seasonal life and gathering places
passages.text: Family hunting territories passed between generations. Rivers and lakes provided routes between them, and seasonal food work combined fishing, hunting, trapping and gathering. Summer meetings brought dispersed families together with neighbouring communities.

passages.title: Seasonal life and gathering places
passages.text: At Apitipik, families celebrated marriages, renewed their belonging to the group and negotiated political alliances. In autumn they returned to their separate hunting territories. Gathering and dispersal were complementary parts of community life.

passages.title: Seasonal life and gathering places
passages.text: Parks Canada describes archaeological evidence of several millennia of occupation at Apitipik, including the Bérubé, Margot and Réal sites. Later trading-post remains add another layer to this landscape. Neither an ancient site nor a trading post supplies a single founding date for the Nation.

passages.title: Pottery and glass beads as evidence
passages.text: A 2009 study examined pottery representing 143 vessels from six Lake Abitibi sites and a private collection. Their Iroquoian characteristics raised questions about relationships with southern Ontario. The style of a pot alone cannot identify the language or ancestry of its maker.

passages.title: Pottery and glass beads as evidence
passages.text: Chloe Lee-Hone’s 2019 research analysed 4,518 glass beads from the Bérubé, Margot and Louis collections. Typological comparisons placed most between about 1600 and 1625 or 1630. These are dates proposed for the beads, not dates for the entire settlements.

passages.title: Pottery and glass beads as evidence
passages.text: At Bérubé, the beads occurred both as a broad scatter and as a dense concentration. Lee-Hone related their movement to exchange between the Huron-Wendat country and French posts on the Saguenay, also examining their role in intercultural relationships. This is an interpretation of objects and historical writing together.

passages.title: Language, images and everyday learning
passages.text: In 2017, Migwan School introduced Nigamou, a songbook and accompanying recording for Anicinabe lessons. Teachers could combine listening, images and singing to help children practise vocabulary. The resource makes language work part of regular classroom activity.

passages.title: Language, images and everyday learning
passages.text: Vocabulary placemats created for families with young children link words with the six Anicinabe seasons, games and recipes. Their format carries teaching into meals and play at home, beyond formal lessons.

passages.title: Language, images and everyday learning
passages.text: The Minawasi community hall’s mural includes the Harricana River, forest, animals, ancestors and a grandmother with her granddaughter. The community describes the pair as an image of knowledge passed to children. Young people participated with local artist Harry Wylde.

passages.title: Language, images and everyday learning
passages.text: Wylde grew up in Pikogan in an artisan family, developed his painting through instruction and independent practice, and later taught young people and adults. His paintings combine Indigenous imagery with landscapes and a distinctive use of backlighting.

passages.title: Community knowledge and environmental research
passages.text: A territory-use interview project began in 2015 to document knowledge, support land claims, identify places needing protection and pass information to future generations. The team also checks information in the field and develops tools for community consultation.

passages.title: Community knowledge and environmental research
passages.text: A collaboration with INRS tests environmental DNA methods in waterways. Traces such as hair, saliva and other material can help researchers investigate wildlife that is difficult to see. The project describes possible future detections, rather than claiming that every sought-after species has already been found.

passages.title: Community knowledge and environmental research
passages.text: The Detour Kesagami caribou population crosses the Québec-Ontario boundary, complicating monitoring. Partners carried out a joint inventory in 2022; that year’s ATIK forum also brought First Nations together to share knowledge, data and resources for caribou protection.

Colonial settlement, logging, mining and residential schooling deeply changed community life. Settlement at Pikogan did not end the Abitibiwinnik. Members continue to use ancestral territories, teach language and knowledge, and pursue their responsibilities to land and future generations. A short interval on the imported map is not a date of cultural disappearance.

sectionTitles: Food, shelter and knowledge of Country
Watercraft and the renewal of skills

passages.text: Tasmanian Aboriginal history belongs to many local peoples, families and Countries across Lutruwita/Tasmania. Their communities developed knowledge suited to changing landscapes and seas, and continue today. This broad map label describes a cultural history, not a single kingdom, and its separated map intervals do not mark the beginning or disappearance of the people.

passages.title: Food, shelter and knowledge of Country
passages.text: Patsy Cameron describes seasonal journeys between coastal and inland food places. Shellfish, crayfish, seabirds and eggs complemented wallaby, other animals and gathered plants. Safe travel by water required knowledge of currents, tides and weather as well as the skill to build a vessel.

passages.title: Food, shelter and knowledge of Country
passages.text: Shelters varied with conditions: domed structures of branches, bark, mud and grass provided protection in cold, windy places, while arched windbreaks served some warmer coastal camps. Fire helped maintain pathways and encourage new vegetation. These practices depended on local knowledge rather than one uniform island-wide routine.

passages.title: What Kutikina’s deposits reveal
passages.text: At Kutikina Cave, Ice Age deposits contained stone artifacts and large quantities of red-necked wallaby bones, including burnt and broken fragments. Layers of charcoal alternated with burnt red clay. Archaeologists interpreted these remains as evidence of repeated hunting, food preparation and fires inside the cave.

passages.title: What Kutikina’s deposits reveal
passages.text: Moser’s study shows why archaeological illustrations need checking. A popular reconstruction included a hand stencil at Kutikina even though none had been found there. The picture combined excavated evidence with details known from other places and later records; the illustration itself cannot prove those details occurred at this cave.

passages.title: Kelp, shells and skilled making
passages.text: A kelp water carrier sent to London’s Great Exhibition in 1851 survives in the British Museum. Its maker’s name was not recorded. The National Museum considers it likely to have come from the people confined at Oyster Cove, preserving both practical knowledge and a history of unequal collecting.

passages.title: Kelp, shells and skilled making
passages.text: Dulcie Greeno’s necklaces combine lustrous maireener shells with smaller rice, button and other shells in carefully arranged strands. Collecting is seasonal work tied to coastal places. Women pass processing and stringing skills between generations while sharing stories and maintaining family relationships.

passages.title: Kelp, shells and skilled making
passages.text: Older shellworking methods used animal-bone tools for piercing, natural fibres or sinew for stringing, and cleaning and polishing to expose the pearly surface. Later steel tools and finer threads enabled makers to incorporate smaller shells. These changes expanded an existing artistic practice.

passages.title: Watercraft and the renewal of skills
passages.text: Early visitors described bark canoes travelling around southern Tasmania and offshore islands. Some carried a hearth at one end. Watercraft helped people reach bird eggs and seal hunting places, linking their construction with everyday food work.

passages.title: Watercraft and the renewal of skills
passages.text: Rex Greeno reconstructed paperbark canoes through reading, experiments with materials and his experience as a fisherman. He made the National Museum’s commissioned canoe with his son and grandson. The object records a deliberate renewal and transmission of skills, rather than uninterrupted survival of an ancient vessel.

passages.title: Voices, language and community action
passages.text: In February 1846, men at Wybalenna petitioned Queen Victoria, asserting that they were free people and that promises made when they left their Country had not been kept. This written petition preserves their own political demands within a record often dominated by colonial officials.

passages.title: Voices, language and community action
passages.text: The Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre’s palawa kani program has worked since the early 1990s to return language to spoken use. Researchers compare wordlists, manuscripts, recordings and remembered family knowledge, checking the reliability of people who originally wrote unfamiliar sounds down.

passages.title: Voices, language and community action
passages.text: Palawa kani draws on evidence from several original Tasmanian languages; it is not an exact restoration of one of them. Community language workers analyse variant spellings and meanings, reconstruct sounds and develop teaching that allows children and adults to use the language together.

passages.title: Voices, language and community action
passages.text: Community leadership has recovered some land and rebuilt institutions for caring for Country. The Aboriginal Land Council describes this work as a result of activism and continuing cultural responsibility, making land management part of contemporary history as well as remembrance.

Colonial invasion brought catastrophic loss of life, dispossession and forced exile. It did not end Tasmanian Aboriginal people. Communities continue across Tasmania and beyond, carrying knowledge through family relationships, cultural practice and renewed institutions. The ending of an imported map interval must not be read as extinction.

passages.text: In February 1846, men at Wybalenna petitioned Queen Victoria, asserting that they were free people and that promises made when they left their Country had not been kept. This written petition preserves their own political demands within a record often dominated by colonial officials.

passages.title: Voices, language and community action
passages.text: The Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre’s palawa kani program has worked since the early 1990s to return language to spoken use. Researchers compare wordlists, manuscripts, recordings and remembered family knowledge, checking the reliability of people who originally wrote unfamiliar sounds down.

passages.title: Voices, language and community action
passages.text: Palawa kani draws on evidence from several original Tasmanian languages; it is not an exact restoration of one of them. Community language workers analyse variant spellings and meanings, reconstruct sounds and develop teaching that allows children and adults to use the language together.

passages.title: Voices, language and community action
passages.text: Community leadership has recovered some land and rebuilt institutions for caring for Country. The Aboriginal Land Council describes this work as a result of activism and continuing cultural responsibility, making land management part of contemporary history as well as remembrance.

Colonial invasion brought catastrophic loss of life, dispossession and forced exile. It did not end Tasmanian Aboriginal people. Communities continue across Tasmania and beyond, carrying knowledge through family relationships, cultural practice and renewed institutions. The ending of an imported map interval must not be read as extinction.

passages.text: Aboriginal peoples of Australia comprise many nations with their own languages, knowledge and relationships to Country. A continent-wide label cannot describe one kingdom or one way of life. The examples here come mainly from the mainland and identify particular places; Torres Strait Islander peoples have distinct histories.

passages.title: Food preparation preserved in stone
passages.text: At Madjedbebe in Mirarr Country, researchers examined grinding stones from deposits spanning the Ice Age and later periods. Wear patterns and chemical residues indicate processing of seeds and other plants. Two stones from the oldest occupation phase, GS39 and GS73, carry evidence interpreted as seed grinding.

passages.title: Food preparation preserved in stone
passages.text: A shaped sandstone whetstone, GS79, occurs in that early phase alongside an axe and flakes removed from ground tools. Together they support the interpretation that people made and maintained sharpened stone edges. Shape alone would be weaker evidence than this combination of objects and wear.

passages.title: Food preparation preserved in stone
passages.text: Red pigments on some stones also indicate grinding, but the researchers rejected many stains as contamination. Surviving pigment does not identify the images once painted, and preservation favours mineral traces over many food residues. An archaeological sample is therefore not a complete picture of daily activity.

passages.title: Engineering a wetland food supply
passages.text: At Budj Bim in south-western Victoria, Gunditjmara builders used volcanic stone to redirect water through channels, dams and weirs. These structures helped trap and hold short-finned eels. Their operation depended on knowledge of water flow and the animals’ seasonal movement.

passages.title: Engineering a wetland food supply
passages.text: Kurtonitj preserves stone house sites, eel traps, channels and trees used for smoking eels. These connected traces show a landscape of food production, processing and settlement. They are specific evidence from Gunditjmara Country, not a template for every Australian environment.

passages.title: Clothing, tools and exchange
passages.text: Wooden boomerangs recovered at Wyrie Swamp in South Australia in 1973 were dated to about 10,000 years ago. They demonstrate ancient woodworking, while their survival cannot establish when the first boomerang was invented. Most Australian boomerangs are not the returning form familiar from popular imagery.

passages.title: Clothing, tools and exchange
passages.text: Boomerangs served as hunting tools, digging implements and percussion instruments, with forms adapted to different tasks. Hooked examples from north-central Australia and heavy carved examples from the Darling and Cooper river systems travelled through exchange networks. Technique and decoration varied among makers and communities.

passages.title: Clothing, tools and exchange
passages.text: People in colder regions made clothing from animal skins. In Noongar language, kangaroo-skin cloaks are called booka. The museum also holds a 2005 reproduction by Lee Darroch and Treahna Hamm of a possum-skin cloak collected at Echuca in 1853, linking practical clothing to cultural renewal.

passages.title: Knowledge and community action
passages.text: Seasonal knowledge guides activities on Country. In recent collaborations, Indigenous knowledge holders and CSIRO have created calendars that communicate local environmental understanding. Ngan’gi, Walmajarri and Kunwinjku projects are distinct examples, not different versions of one national calendar.

passages.title: Knowledge and community action
passages.text: From 1792, Pemulwuy led resistance near the Parramatta, Hawkesbury and Georges rivers. His actions and the punitive colonial response show that occupation was contested. This Sydney-region history should not be assigned automatically to distant communities with different experiences of invasion.

passages.title: Knowledge and community action
passages.text: The 1967 campaign drew on petitions, community organising and alliances. Joe McGinness and Faith Bandler were among its leading organisers. The resulting constitutional change did not first grant voting rights: the federal franchise had already been extended in 1962.

Colonisation brought profound losses of land, lives and self-government, but Aboriginal peoples did not disappear. Communities continue in urban, regional and remote Australia, maintaining and renewing distinct identities. A change or ending in this broad map label records the atlas’s categories, not a single surrender or the end of a people.

passages.text: Ethiopia’s history includes a long-lived empire and later governments, alongside communities with distinct languages, religions and institutions. Abyssinia was a European name used for the empire. Manuscripts, buildings, farming landscapes and living craft traditions reveal histories that cannot be reduced to the careers of emperors.

passages.title: Books as objects of knowledge
passages.text: A Gospel manuscript now at the Metropolitan Museum dates from the late fourteenth or early fifteenth century. Its parchment pages combine Ge’ez text with painted Gospel scenes. The museum identifies two artists, whose shared visual language transformed models connected to the eastern Mediterranean.

passages.title: Books as objects of knowledge
passages.text: The book was made at a northern Ethiopian monastic centre. A possible connection to Dabra Hayg Estifanos is a scholarly attribution, not a recorded excavation find. Notes associate its recipient church with the Archangel Michael, while the paintings were intended for viewing during worship and processions.

passages.title: Books as objects of knowledge
passages.text: The late seventeenth-century Arganonä Maryam prayer book organises prayers using decorated headings for days of the week. Geometric borders help readers navigate the text. Its parchment, pigments, script and binding required several kinds of practical skill as well as religious learning.

passages.title: Books as objects of knowledge
passages.text: Pencil additions, erased and rewritten red text, and smudges reveal the prayer book’s later use. Its colophon names Baselyos, but scholars debate whether the scribe also painted the hornbill image associated with this group of manuscripts. Evidence of authorship is therefore more complex than one modern artist label.

passages.title: Buildings and water management
passages.text: Fasil Ghebbi’s royal compound contains more than castles. Its surviving structures include a library, a chancellery and a banqueting hall, alongside palaces and nearby churches. The ensemble shows how a settled court brought administration, ceremony and skilled construction into a permanent urban centre.

passages.title: Buildings and water management
passages.text: At the Bath of Fasilidas, a canal carried water from the nearby river into a rectangular pool around a pavilion. The building stands on pier arches and was reached by a stone bridge. Water supply and structural engineering were integral to the royal landscape.

passages.title: Farming, households and collective work
passages.text: Konso communities shaped steep land with dry-stone terraces that retain soil, collect rainfall and discharge excess water. Their maintenance depends on organised communal labour. These southern Ethiopian landscapes represent local environmental knowledge rather than a technology that can be credited to the imperial dynasty.

passages.title: Farming, households and collective work
passages.text: Within Konso settlements, communal spaces called moras organise social and ceremonial life. Reservoirs are built and maintained collectively, while generation-marking stones record transfers of responsibility. Farming infrastructure and local institutions belong to the same cultural landscape.

passages.title: Textiles, skill and contemporary livelihoods
passages.text: Designer Hana Getachew describes Habesha dresses made from fine cotton with coloured geometric decoration called tibeb. On a simple two-harness loom, artisans must pick decorative patterns by hand or add embroidery. The cloth’s apparent lightness conceals patient, technically demanding work.

passages.title: Textiles, skill and contemporary livelihoods
passages.text: At the contemporary Sabahar workshop, local women spin cotton by hand, yarn is dyed, and weavers thread the loom before weaving panels. Washing and careful stitching finish the cloth. Getachew’s account links design, distributed labour and changing markets without implying that all Ethiopian households follow this practice.

passages.title: Institutions beyond the palace
passages.text: The Oromo Gada system provides a distinct tradition of community governance. Assemblies and elected leadership address administration, disputes and social responsibilities, while knowledge is passed between generations. It operates at a local level and should not be confused with the institutions of Ethiopia’s imperial or federal governments.

passages.title: Institutions beyond the palace
passages.text: Haile Selassie’s 1931 constitution drew on foreign constitutional models but strengthened imperial authority. Written government rules did not necessarily mean independent parliamentary power. This distinction helps explain why institutional reform and political participation did not always advance together.

passages.title: Expansion, resistance and political change
passages.text: Menelik II’s army defeated the Italian invasion at Adwa in 1896. His reign also brought conquest and annexation in the south. Resistance to European colonial rule and expansion over neighbouring communities were different processes within the same imperial history.

passages.title: Expansion, resistance and political change
passages.text: The constitution adopted in December 1994 speaks in the name of Ethiopia’s nations, nationalities and peoples, emphasising equality and shared political life. Its wording records the new constitutional project; it is not proof that subsequent governments fulfilled every stated aim.

The emperor was removed in September 1974 and the Derg assumed power. That ended imperial government, not Ethiopia or its peoples. The Derg itself fell in 1991, followed by a transitional administration and a federal republic. These regime changes must be distinguished from the country’s continuing history.

sectionTitles: A waterfront town and its carpentry

passages.text: Peninsular Nova Scotia became a British colonial territory within Mi’kma’ki, the homeland of the Mi’kmaq. Its history includes Acadian farming, forced displacement, port towns and diverse migrant communities. The peninsula shown by this map record belongs to Nova Scotia; the colony’s larger boundaries changed over time.

passages.title: Farming with the tides
passages.text: Acadian dykes used wooden sluices called aboiteaux. At low tide, freshwater drained outward; rising seawater pushed a valve shut. Rain and melting snow gradually removed salt from the enclosed ground, allowing cultivation. The system adapted earlier techniques to the Bay of Fundy’s demanding tidal environment.

passages.title: Farming with the tides
passages.text: Wheat, oats and flax grew on reclaimed land. Roads could run along dyke tops, with oxen or horses pulling carts. Water management therefore shaped both food production and everyday movement, while continued maintenance was essential to protecting the fields.

passages.title: Farming with the tides
passages.text: At Melanson, rectangular depressions and grassy mounds preserve traces interpreted as collapsed chimneys or ovens. Circular mounds may mark wells, mills and other structures. Eighteenth-century engineers’ plans help researchers connect these features to a family-based settlement, while some individual functions remain uncertain.

passages.title: Farming with the tides
passages.text: After deportation, Planter settlement overlaid the Acadian landscape at Grand-Pré. The newcomers used its established drainage technology. Continuity of farmland must therefore be distinguished from continuity of ownership or an absence of forced displacement.

passages.title: Discoveries at Birchtown
passages.text: Excavation of the late eighteenth-century site AkDi 12 revealed a cellar-like feature. Initially interpreted as a root cellar, it was later understood as a temporary dwelling used around the first winter of Black Loyalist settlement in 1783. That interpretation links household remains to the difficulties of establishing shelter.

passages.title: Discoveries at Birchtown
passages.text: At AkDi 23, archaeologists recovered ceramics, matched dish sets, military buttons, a bayonet and a boarding axe. They associated the assemblage with Stephen Blucke’s property on the basis of its character and quality. The attribution is an archaeological argument, not proof supplied by the objects alone.

passages.title: Discoveries at Birchtown
passages.text: Birchtown residents worked in fishing, woodcutting, land clearing, domestic service and day labour. Black settlers received smaller grants and provisions, or none, and faced lower wages. Meanwhile, some white Loyalists brought enslaved people, so freedom and slavery coexisted in colonial Nova Scotia.

passages.title: Discoveries at Birchtown
passages.text: The 1792 emigrants carried tools, furniture, muskets and spinning wheels to Sierra Leone. Such belongings show the practical resources families valued when moving again. Other community members, including teachers and ship pilots, remained in Nova Scotia.

passages.title: A waterfront town and its carpentry
passages.text: Lunenburg was laid out in 1753 on a rectangular street grid. Its surviving wooden houses and public buildings, property divisions and working waterfront preserve the organisation of a colonial town whose economy was closely tied to offshore fishing. The plan and the buildings are related evidence of urban life.

passages.title: A waterfront town and its carpentry
passages.text: Benjamin Knaut’s house, built in 1793 to 1794, combined a New England Colonial exterior with a Georgian interior plan. It belonged to a substantial estate with gardens and an orchard. As a merchant’s home, it records wealth and skilled building, not the housing conditions of every resident.

passages.title: A waterfront town and its carpentry
passages.text: Conrad Rhuland, a mariner and privateer, bought the house in 1813 and changed its front parlour in a regional German vernacular style. The building’s successive alterations show how residents adapted inherited structures rather than preserving a single untouched colonial moment.

passages.title: Treaties and changing colonial boundaries
passages.text: The Mi’kmawey Debert Cultural Centre explains the Peace and Friendship Treaties as reciprocal agreements involving trade, settlement and distinct legal authorities. They did not surrender Mi’kmaq territory. Colonial control on a map must therefore not be read as a treaty cession of Indigenous land.

passages.title: Treaties and changing colonial boundaries
passages.text: In 1784, New Brunswick and Cape Breton became separate colonies from Nova Scotia; Cape Breton rejoined it in 1820. These administrative changes explain why a map of the peninsula cannot stand for the whole colony at every date.

Nova Scotia entered the Canadian federation in 1867 as a province. This was a constitutional transformation, not a military fall or the disappearance of its communities. Confederation also did not immediately end Canada’s relationship of dependence on Britain. The map’s 1815 endpoint is only the end of this imported label’s coverage.

sectionTitles: Colonial disruption and choices under pressure

passages.text: Acaxee communities lived in the rugged Sierra de Topia, mainly in present-day Durango and partly in Sinaloa. The name covers dispersed communities rather than a single kingdom. Their history combines farming, mountain resources, local institutions and resistance to Spanish colonial intrusion.

passages.title: Mountain livelihoods and skilled work
passages.text: Families cultivated maize, beans, squash and chillies on small plots where the terrain permitted. Hunting, river fishing and gathered plants supplemented harvests. This mixed economy connected cultivable patches with the surrounding mountains rather than depending on one crop alone.

passages.title: Mountain livelihoods and skilled work
passages.text: Wild maguey supplied ixtle fibre as well as fermented drinks. Clothing included decorated fibre cloth and prepared animal skins. These materials required knowledge of local plants and animals, linking everyday dress to the resources of the sierra.

passages.title: Mountain livelihoods and skilled work
passages.text: Extended-family settlements were politically independent. Ortega describes cooperation under a chosen leader for particular military actions, rather than a permanent authority governing every community. A continuous shaded territory on a map should not be mistaken for a centralised Acaxee state.

passages.title: Mountain livelihoods and skilled work
passages.text: Pérez de Ribas describes stone-and-mud houses and timber houses with straw roofs around Topia. Larger communal buildings also served defensive purposes. His account preserves descriptions from around 1600, although published later; it is missionary testimony, not an excavated building catalogue.

passages.title: Mountain livelihoods and skilled work
passages.text: The same account records strings of white shells obtained from coastal peoples and worn as ornaments. It also describes teaching with stones arranged to represent successive prayers. The mnemonic practice shows local methods of learning being adapted within mission instruction.

passages.title: What regional archaeology reveals
passages.text: Cueva del Maguey, above the San Pedro River in southern Durango, offers evidence from the broader highland world. Researchers place the regional Protoxixime phase at about 1350 to 1600. Its remains should not automatically be labelled Acaxee: archaeological traditions and historically named peoples do not align with certainty.

passages.title: What regional archaeology reveals
passages.text: Excavations there in 2008 to 2010 recovered domestic structures made with a framework and earthen infill, interior benches and hearths, bowls, pots and grinding stones. Food remains and chemical residues helped researchers identify cooking, storage and possible outdoor eating areas. These are interpretations supported by several kinds of evidence.

passages.title: What regional archaeology reveals
passages.text: Structure 10 in Cave 4 contained maize cobs and a grinding handstone near a bench. Stone tools and resin also suggest craft activity. The room may have served several purposes; neither one object nor a patch of residue establishes a single, exclusive household function.

passages.title: Colonial disruption and choices under pressure
passages.text: Silver mining brought severe labour demands, while epidemics and campaigns against Indigenous religious objects intensified colonial pressure. Delgadillo’s study connects these conditions with resistance. Mission records must be read critically because their authors sought to justify conversion and colonial authority.

passages.title: Colonial disruption and choices under pressure
passages.text: Some Acaxee households moved to rancherías away from European settlements. Missionaries also offered tools, food and positions of authority to attract converts. Acceptance of baptism therefore cannot by itself show that every older belief or community relationship had been abandoned.

Spanish conquest, mission concentration, coercive labour and disease progressively undermined Acaxee autonomy. Delgadillo describes the erosion of a distinct cultural identity through the colonial period, reaching the eighteenth century. This does not establish that every descendant disappeared. The imported map endpoint of 1650 is neither a documented extinction date nor a single fall of an Acaxee kingdom.

passages.text: The Accomac were Indigenous communities of the southern Delmarva Peninsula, on Virginia’s Eastern Shore. Related to neighbouring Algonquian-speaking peoples, they maintained settlements, farming and exchange across a landscape of creeks and coastal resources. Their history is distinct from that of the later county and town bearing similar names.

passages.title: Food, settlements and exchange
passages.text: Southern Delmarva offered cultivable sandy soils alongside birds, fish and shellfish. Researchers propose that Accomac households sometimes dispersed to gather food while crops ripened. This is a reconstruction of seasonal practice, not a surviving calendar specifying what every family did in each month.

passages.title: Food, settlements and exchange
passages.text: Accomac settlements occupied river drainages rather than one compact capital. Permanent settlement could include dispersed households and hamlets. A European visitor’s preference for describing dense villages can therefore distort how much organisation existed in a less visibly clustered landscape.

passages.title: Food, settlements and exchange
passages.text: The Accomac and Occohannock paid shell beads as tribute to Powhatan while retaining their harvests. Beads thus mattered beyond decoration: exchange arrangements affected how much food communities could keep. The relationship across Chesapeake Bay was political and economic, not simply geographic proximity.

passages.title: Food, settlements and exchange
passages.text: Researchers associate Accomac material culture with Townsend pottery in the broader Slaughter Creek archaeological complex. This classification links patterns in finds with historical accounts. It is not proof that any isolated Townsend sherd belonged to a named Accomac person or settlement.

passages.title: Food, settlements and exchange
passages.text: The Gingaskin reservation supported farming, hunting and fishing. By the eighteenth century, portions were leased to outsiders as land pressure increased. These changing arrangements show households navigating both older subsistence practices and a colonial property economy.

passages.title: Discoveries in the written record
passages.text: Land transactions first name Debedeavon in 1648 as a ruler in the more northerly Occohannock region and record him again in 1664. The Library of Virginia distinguishes him from the earlier southern chief called the Laughing King. Combining them creates a false biography.

passages.title: Discoveries in the written record
passages.text: The chief visited by Smith in 1608 was unnamed in his account. Pory’s 1621 description does not establish that the Laughing King was the same man. Later monuments made the identification seem settled, illustrating why inscriptions must be checked against the records they claim to commemorate.

passages.title: Discoveries in the written record
passages.text: Patents and boundary disputes trace the reservation’s contraction: the Library of Virginia describes an initial 1,500 acres and a later patent for 650 acres in 1680. These documents record colonial recognition of a shrinking land base, not the beginning of Accomac occupation.

passages.title: Discoveries in the written record
passages.text: Petitions in 1784 and 1787 attacked Gingaskin rights by claiming intermarriage meant that no Indians remained. Those claims served outsiders seeking the land. They are evidence of racial classification being used for dispossession, rather than neutral evidence that the community had ceased to exist.

passages.title: Land loss and living contributions
passages.text: The reservation’s trustees supported dividing community land into individually saleable plots. After the 1813 law, later pressure following Nat Turner’s 1831 uprising displaced many owners. The sequence separates legal allotment from the subsequent breakup of the settlement.

passages.title: Land loss and living contributions
passages.text: Writer and scholar Ron Welburn identifies Gingaskin ancestry among his family’s several heritages. His work includes poetry, Eastern Native literature, oral history and jazz studies, and he helped establish a Native American studies programme. His career is a documented example of descendant cultural contribution.

Virginia’s 1813 allotment law ended communal reservation ownership, and later displacement fractured the Gingaskin settlement. It did not erase all descendants. Welburn’s documented ancestry and cultural work are one example of continuity beyond the reservation. The map’s 1500 endpoint is only imported coverage and cannot mark the end of Accomac history.

passages.text: British rule joined the coastal Gold Coast colony and several differently administered territories under a changing constitutional framework. The history of the communities living there is much broader than colonial government. Farmers, fishers, potters, traders, teachers and writers shaped the society that became independent Ghana.

passages.title: Buildings and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: Coastal forts such as Ussher and James in Accra and Christiansborg in Osu predate the formal British colony. Their courtyards, bastions, storerooms and accommodation reveal how commercial and military functions were combined within enclosed compounds. Their architecture records repeated occupation and adaptation by different European powers.

passages.title: Buildings and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: The forts served trade in gold and later the Atlantic traffic in enslaved Africans. Their survival is evidence of those coercive systems and the international networks surrounding them. They are not simply monuments to construction skill or neutral symbols of overseas exchange.

passages.title: Buildings and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: At Christiansborg, archaeologists working with descendant communities found house foundations, local and imported ceramics, beads and smoking pipes. Three stones with charcoal suggested a cooking area, but that identification is interpretive. These discoveries bring nearby households into a history often told only through the castle.

passages.title: Buildings and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: Pottery studied from the 2016 Christiansborg garden excavations includes soot-marked vessels consistent with cooking. Stepped rims may have supported lids. The report had not yet obtained chronometric dates, so its broad post-seventeenth-century context does not justify assigning each sherd to a particular colonial year.

passages.title: Buildings and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: Incised bowls known as weika are compared with vessels used to grind condiments, while other forms served food or carried liquids. These functional comparisons help reconstruct household work, but vessel shapes could have overlapping uses. A surviving fragment does not identify the exact meal once prepared in it.

passages.title: Buildings and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: Regional pottery traditions include hand coiling, apprenticeship and open firing. Engmann uses those traditions as comparisons, not direct observation of the excavated pots’ manufacture. Clay suitable for pottery is scarce at Osu, and the origins of most recovered vessels remain uncertain.

passages.title: Fishing, innovation and coastal livelihoods
passages.text: Fishing supported an extensive division of labour. Men generally worked at sea, while women processed catches and organised trade into inland markets. Women also advocated more productive nets. Decisions about equipment therefore affected fishers, processors and traders differently, rather than benefiting a single undifferentiated community.

passages.title: Fishing, innovation and coastal livelihoods
passages.text: African entrepreneurs developed and adapted large ali drift nets and yevudor beach seines. Accounts disagree over their first introduction. From 1898 to 1923, disputes concerned juvenile fish, declining catches, prices and the larger rewards claimed by equipment owners. More productive technology also raised questions about conservation and access to earnings.

passages.title: Cocoa farming and scientific work
passages.text: Tetteh Quarshie, a blacksmith from Osu, returned from Fernando Po with cocoa in 1879 and cultivated it at Akwapim Mampong. Farmers obtained pods from his farm and spread cultivation. Earlier Dutch and missionary introductions mean that his contribution is better understood as successful propagation than the first arrival of cocoa.

passages.title: Cocoa farming and scientific work
passages.text: From 1886, the Aburi Botanical Garden also supplied cocoa planting material. Expansion depended on farmers establishing and tending trees as well as these distribution networks. The crop’s spread was a process of agricultural adoption involving many cultivators, not the work of one planter alone.

passages.title: Cocoa farming and scientific work
passages.text: The Central Cocoa Research Station opened at Akim Tafo in 1938 to investigate pests and diseases affecting farms. Its successor, the West African Cocoa Research Institute, expanded the programme in 1944 to include soils and cultivation practices. Scientific investigation developed around practical problems in a major agricultural livelihood.

passages.title: Education, print and political change
passages.text: Achimota opened in 1927 and developed school, teacher-training and higher-education branches. Its curriculum brought science and vocational work together with art, music and African dance. The institution provides a concrete example of education combining technical preparation and cultural expression, without implying that such opportunities were available to every child.

passages.title: Education, print and political change
passages.text: The University of Ghana preserves a catalogue record for Gold Coast Leader issues from April to July 1907, published at Cape Coast. Its description identifies local and international political and social reporting. This archival record documents a local newspaper culture; it does not establish the views of every resident.

passages.title: Education, print and political change
passages.text: The Ghana Independence Act ended British governmental responsibility for the new country from 6 March 1957. It also restricted future British legislation for Ghana to measures requested and consented to by Ghana. The legal change concerned sovereignty, not the disappearance of the communities previously governed as colonial subjects.

The colonial constitutional order gave way to independent Ghana on 6 March 1957. The Gold Coast name and British responsibility ended; the population, settlements and working traditions continued into a new political history. The map’s earlier record endpoints are coverage boundaries, not separate dates of national independence.
