passages.text: The Achaemenid Empire, founded by Cyrus the Great in 550 BCE, was the largest state the world had seen, reaching from the Balkans and Egypt to the Indus. Its kings ruled dozens of peoples through satraps, roads and a common administrative language, and mostly let them keep their gods and laws.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Royal Road ran about 2,700 kilometers from Susa to Sardis; Herodotus says a traveler took ninety days and a relay of royal couriers about a week.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Qanats, tunnels that carry groundwater out to the plains, spread across Iran under the empire.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Darius I struck the gold daric and the silver siglos, the first coins used across the whole empire.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Darius began Persepolis, with its terrace, hundred-columned halls, bull capitals and staircases carved with tribute-bearers from every province.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay text from Babylon, records Cyrus restoring temples and sending deported peoples home; the modern description of it as a charter of human rights is disputed by historians.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The kings invoked Ahura Mazda in their inscriptions; how far the court followed Zoroaster's teaching is debated.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Cyrus let the Judean exiles in Babylon return to Jerusalem and rebuild the Temple, as the Hebrew Bible records.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Some twenty satrapies paid tribute in silver and kind, each under a governor watched by the king's inspectors.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Roads, coinage and a long peace tied the Mediterranean to Central Asia and India.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Imperial Aramaic served as the language of administration from Egypt to Bactria.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Later Iranian dynasties, the Sasanians above all, looked back to the Achaemenids.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Alexander and the Seleucids kept the satrapies and much of the administration.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Persepolis was listed by UNESCO.
Alexander defeated Darius III at Gaugamela in 331 BCE and burned Persepolis in 330. Darius was killed by his own satrap the same year, and Alexander took the empire as its heir.

sectionTitles: Craft and exchange in the historical record

passages.text: The Achagua are an Indigenous people of Colombia’s Orinoco region, with continuing communities at Umapo and El Turpial. Their history connects riverine exchange, cassava cultivation, household cooperation and an Arawakan language maintained through everyday use and teaching.

passages.title: Craft and exchange in the historical record
passages.text: Quiripa beads were made by shaping freshwater shells into small discs, perforating them and stringing them together. Achagua craftspeople were among several peoples producing them. The process turned local material into a portable means of payment and a visible marker of prestige.

passages.title: Craft and exchange in the historical record
passages.text: Quiripa circulated beyond the plains into the Andes and Guiana. The historical synthesis warns that a uniform exchange value for a string has not been established. Calling it currency should therefore not imply one centrally regulated coinage or an unchanging price across the region.

passages.title: Craft and exchange in the historical record
passages.text: Trade also intersected with violence: accounts describe Achagua captives being exchanged for quiripa. Beads demonstrate neither peaceful commerce alone nor an isolated economy. Their history includes both skilled manufacture and the exploitation of people within expanding exchange networks.

passages.title: Food and household work
passages.text: Bitter cassava is a major crop. Achagua households process it into casabe flatbread and toasted fariña, alongside growing maize. Fishing becomes particularly important in the dry season. Food production combines cultivation, processing skill and attention to changing river conditions.

passages.title: Food and household work
passages.text: ONIC describes households organised around an older couple, their younger children and married daughters’ families. Sons-in-law may build separate homes as the group grows. Residence, food production and consumption are connected through this family organisation rather than being isolated household choices.

passages.title: Language, learning and participation
passages.text: Children learn Achagua with parents, grandparents and other relatives while farming, fishing and making crafts. The Ministry of Culture’s study treats these activities as settings for education. Practical knowledge and language are transmitted together, rather than only through formal classroom lessons.

passages.title: Language, learning and participation
passages.text: The study describes leaders coordinating community activities in Achagua. When outside meetings use Spanish or Piapoco, interpretation helps elders participate. Multilingual communication is therefore an institutional skill, while the continued use of Achagua supports involvement by people who do not readily use those other languages.

passages.title: Language, learning and participation
passages.text: Indigenous teachers use Achagua at school alongside other language learning. Grammars, a bilingual dictionary and reading materials provide written resources, although the study identifies shortages. Maintaining a language involves new educational work as well as the continuity of speech at home.

passages.title: Recording and renewing community knowledge
passages.text: Research at Umapo gathered accounts from knowledge holders and worked with families and Yaaliakeisy students. Its interviews and workshops provide direct evidence of how participants remembered and taught traditions. The small local study cannot measure the knowledge of every Achagua community.

passages.title: Recording and renewing community knowledge
passages.text: Knowledge holders recounted Chumachumarri, a tree associated with the origin of foods, and described other narratives linking people and nature. The researchers recorded these as community traditions. They are evidence of ways of explaining the world, not independently dated accounts of prehistoric events.

passages.title: Recording and renewing community knowledge
passages.text: Students used modelling clay and posters to explore identity. Community participants also helped shape a learning room for sharing narratives at Yaaliakeisy. The project created a concrete educational space, while acknowledging disagreements and uneven interest in transmitting older traditions.

Achagua history continues through living communities, language and educational work. Changes in belief and livelihood do not amount to the disappearance of the people. The imported map’s 1500 endpoint records the end of a snapshot interval, not an Achagua extinction or conquest.

sectionTitles: Historical records and the return of ancestors

passages.text: The Aché are Indigenous communities of eastern Paraguay whose histories include forest hunting and gathering, violent dispossession, settlement and continuing cultural work. Research on Northern Aché families documents practical knowledge, cooperation and changing livelihoods; it should not be treated as a description of every Aché community.

passages.title: Tools, materials and skilled manufacture
passages.text: A child’s bow from Arroyo Bandera, now in the Museo de América, was made before 1997. Its slightly curved wooden body carries a twisted plant-fibre string secured around both ends. The object preserves the combination of carving, cord-making and binding needed to produce working equipment.

passages.title: Tools, materials and skilled manufacture
passages.text: The museum names the bow rapa and records separate Aché terms for its wood and cord fibre. Its account also describes using an unstrung bow to reach animals in burrows. Such versatility connects tool design with detailed knowledge of different hunting situations.

passages.title: Tools, materials and skilled manufacture
passages.text: An Aché arrow at the Spencer Museum combines bamboo, wood, plant fibre, resin and feathers tentatively identified as guan. Its maker is unrecorded, and its date spans the late nineteenth century to 1976. The catalogue supports a study of material selection, not an exact manufacturing year or excavated findspot.

passages.title: Food, work and cooperation
passages.text: At Chupa Pou in 1981 to 1982, researchers observed maize, manioc, beans, peanuts and other crops. Groups cleared and planted large fields, while some men began smaller plots. Farming arrangements were changing within the settlement itself, rather than representing a timeless Aché agricultural system.

passages.title: Food, work and cooperation
passages.text: The same fieldwork describes men and women moving a temporary brush barricade through a lagoon to concentrate fish. Springs supplied domestic water, while rivers and streams served washing and bathing. These observations connect collective fishing skill with the practical organisation of settlement life.

passages.title: Food, work and cooperation
passages.text: Forest foods in the Northern Aché studies included hunted mammals, honey, palm starch, fruit and larvae. Obtaining a meal required several kinds of work and knowledge. Researchers describe different contributions by men and women, with patterns tied to the studied trips and households rather than universal rules.

passages.title: Food, work and cooperation
passages.text: Food gathered on forest trips was distributed widely between families, particularly meat and honey. The authors compared those trips with life at Arroyo Bandera in 1998, where food was more often directed toward families who shared similar foods back. Cooperation changed with residence and production.

passages.title: Food, work and cooperation
passages.text: Settlement livelihoods also included paid work and occasional sales of palm-woven fans, mats, bows and arrows. Purchased foods and tools entered household economies alongside farming and forest resources. Cultural continuity could include participating in new markets, rather than preserving one fixed way of obtaining everything.

passages.title: Historical records and the return of ancestors
passages.text: Paraguay’s Indigenous-community census history describes captures and a massacre between 1959 and 1972, followed by international denunciations in 1974. The violent breakup of forest communities cannot be described simply as voluntary modernisation. The record identifies assaults on people, not the end of Aché existence.

passages.title: Historical records and the return of ancestors
passages.text: Archival research reconstructed the fate of an Aché girl called Damiana, abducted in 1897 and taken to Argentina. After her death, remains entered scientific collections associated with racial investigation. Letters and publications helped identify material later located in Berlin, exposing violence within the history of collecting.

passages.title: Historical records and the return of ancestors
passages.text: La Plata returned remains to the Aché community in 2010; Berlin returned further identified remains in 2012. The researchers explicitly recognised the community’s wish for burial. These events changed the relationship between institutions and the people whose ancestors they had held.

passages.title: Language and community authorship
passages.text: In August 2025, teachers and representatives from six Aché communities met at Cerro Morotĩ to review and correct a dictionary draft. Community members and LETRA Paraguay had developed the material together. This was active editorial and linguistic work, not merely outsiders recording passive informants.

passages.title: Language and community authorship
passages.text: The national language secretariat’s digital vocabulary page credits members of the Aché people as authors and LETRA Paraguay as compiler. Online and mobile resources extend language work into new media. Their availability documents a continuing language project without establishing how widely each resource is used.

Aché communities survived campaigns of capture and violence and continue to maintain language and collective institutions. Dispossession transformed residence and livelihoods, but it did not produce a historical extinction date. The imported map ends at 1500 because its snapshot interval ends there, not because Aché history stopped.

passages.text: The Maya Achi are living communities of Guatemala’s Baja Verapaz region. Rabinal is an important centre of their cultural life, where textile work and community teaching remain active. The history of the people is broader than any single archaeological town, dramatic character or political regime.

passages.title: Discovering settlements and working landscapes
passages.text: Surveyors mapped Saq’ijel, a Postclassic town only somewhat smaller than Cahyup, in the hills above Rabinal. Residential areas and ceremonial centres occupied a landscape with several substantial communities. This evidence challenges a picture in which all local life revolved around one isolated capital.

passages.title: Discovering settlements and working landscapes
passages.text: The researchers placed fields on the basin floor and settlements on higher slopes. They proposed irrigation from upland springs, but had not systematically surveyed the lowlands. Their reconstruction links land, water and settlement while preserving the difference between mapped remains and a plausible farming model.

passages.title: Making pottery and supplying households
passages.text: In Álvarez’s Rabinal field study, potters prepared clay brought from nearby hills and built vessel walls with coils, using a broken pot as a support. Larger vessels were worked by moving around them. Smaller ones could be rotated on the maker’s knees, showing how technique adapted to scale.

passages.title: Making pottery and supplying households
passages.text: Potters shaped and smoothed bases, added necks, and applied red clay mixed with water before firing. Finished pots and pitchers were sold by their makers in the plaza. These observations connect household technology with market livelihoods; they do not establish an unchanged method stretching back to prehistory.

passages.title: Making pottery and supplying households
passages.text: The study also records censers, candlesticks and small figures representing occupations such as carrying, milling and selling. Some objects served ceremonies while others depicted daily work. Families participated in production, and goods travelled to markets beyond Rabinal as well as being sold locally.

passages.title: Textile design and teaching
passages.text: An unfinished Rabinal huipil in the British Museum combines a dark cotton ground, narrow coloured warp stripes and brocaded zigzags and triangles. The decoration required complex weaving even where the design appears simple. The catalogue dates the cloth only to before 1973.

passages.title: Textile design and teaching
passages.text: The same garment uses a single wide panel. Brocading was omitted where its future owner would cut the neck opening, so the unfinished cloth preserves a decision made for later assembly and wear. This is a collected textile from Rabinal, not a fabric recovered from an ancient building.

passages.title: Textile design and teaching
passages.text: A Rabinal workshop in late 2025 brought children, young people and adults together with cultural practitioners from Pacux. Participants used winding and warping tools and counting techniques to make huipils and other textiles. An exhibition displayed the results, documenting a specific effort to pass skills between generations.

passages.title: Theatre, music and collective memory
passages.text: Rabinal Achí combines spoken narrative, masked dance and music. UNESCO traces its development to the fifteenth century. Its conflict between Rabinal Achí and K’iche’ Achí stages political authority and obligations, while its performance preserves an artistic tradition rather than proving every narrated incident occurred exactly as shown.

passages.title: Theatre, music and collective memory
passages.text: Since colonial times, performances have formed part of the January feast of Saint Paul. Cofradías, local religious brotherhoods, coordinate the festival. Sustaining the drama therefore requires institutions, preparation and community responsibilities as well as the knowledge of individual performers.

passages.title: Theatre, music and collective memory
passages.text: Masks represent ancestral beings, linking participants with the dead and with future generations. UNESCO also identifies poverty and the reduction of the drama to spectacle as threats. Preserving the performance involves its meanings and relationships, not only keeping costumes or repeating dance movements.

passages.title: Survival and community institutions
passages.text: The Rabinal memory museum grew from local organising and a temporary exhibition in 1999. Its founders describe remembrance of army and paramilitary violence as central to its purpose. Exhibitions and educational activities aim to dignify survivors and strengthen younger people’s understanding of their history.

The Maya Achi continue as living communities. Mass violence devastated their lives without erasing the people. Rabinal’s community museum explicitly joins remembrance of loss with cultural renewal. The map’s 1500 endpoint is only the end of imported coverage.

sectionTitles: What the written record can reveal

passages.text: The Achire were Indigenous coastal communities in what is now Sinaloa, Mexico. Accounts place them among the marshes and fisheries of the Pacific coast. Their history concerns mobile households and practical coastal knowledge, rather than a documented empire with a single capital.

passages.title: Plant fibres and coastal technology
passages.text: Ortega’s account describes Guasave and Achire people weaving straw and tule into baskets. Plant fibres became containers through skilled handling of local materials. The description is documentary evidence of a craft, not the identification of a basket excavated from a securely dated Achire site.

passages.title: Plant fibres and coastal technology
passages.text: The same account records small woven rafts used near the shore. Their scale and coastal use matter: this supports knowledge of local navigation, but does not establish ocean crossings or a fleet of large boats. Rafts and baskets represent distinct applications of plant-fibre technology.

passages.title: Food, movement and exchange
passages.text: Historical descriptions place related people together in mobile groups and describe fishing, shellfish gathering, hunting and wild fruits as central to subsistence. Their movements connected several food sources across the marshes; mobility should not be mistaken for the absence of social organisation.

passages.title: Food, movement and exchange
passages.text: Baena Reina’s reading of Mota y Escobar records fish and shellfish exchanged with settled neighbours for maize and beans. These exchanges linked coastal harvesting with farming communities. Access to cultivated foods therefore does not, by itself, prove that the Achire grew those crops.

passages.title: Food, movement and exchange
passages.text: The same study places Achire movements between the Guayabal area and the coast near the Mocorito River. Travelling with portable possessions suited this way of using the shoreline. The route is a description of movement, not a surveyed boundary of an exclusive territorial state.

passages.title: What the written record can reveal
passages.text: The municipal history identifies an Achire settlement in a report dated 1605, more than a century after the map’s imported endpoint. It supplies a concrete locality and date for examining colonial encounters, while leaving the settlement’s size and internal layout unspecified.

passages.title: What the written record can reveal
passages.text: The bishop’s language, reproduced in the later scholarship, disparaged the communities he described. His observations about trade and movement can be examined without adopting that ranking of peoples. The account conveys a colonial observer’s perspective; it is not an Achire account of their own lives.

passages.title: What the written record can reveal
passages.text: Villalobos Fernández distinguishes a short discussion of Guasave and Achire communities from a much wider survey of fishing implements. Illustrations from central Mexican manuscripts and descriptions of other fisheries do not automatically identify Achire equipment. The wider comparisons must remain separate from specifically attributed practices.

The sources checked here do not establish a dated end to Achire communities or a verified present-day successor identity. Their later history needs further documentary tracing. The imported map’s 1500 endpoint cannot represent their disappearance: the municipal history explicitly records Achire inhabitants in 1605.

passages.text: Acho Dene Koe is a living Dene First Nation centred at Fort Liard. Its traditional territory and waters extend across the Northwest Territories, British Columbia and Yukon, with relationships to François Lake as well. Modern jurisdictional boundaries do not encompass the whole of this homeland.

passages.title: Water, food and seasonal knowledge
passages.text: The Liard River serves different forms of travel across the year. Community knowledge describes canoes and other boats on open water, and dog teams on the frozen river. The same corridor connects fishing places, camps and neighbouring communities as its surface changes with the season.

passages.title: Water, food and seasonal knowledge
passages.text: Fish are eaten fresh, smoked or dried, and some catches feed working dogs. The seasonal account describes autumn storage in raised caches and winter net fishing through ice. Two survey participants also described distributing surplus fish to Elders, linking harvesting with responsibilities to other people.

passages.title: Water, food and seasonal knowledge
passages.text: The Nation’s 2021 study collected knowledge from five members through a survey adapted to pandemic restrictions. It recorded fishing practices and observations of environmental change to support future monitoring. These findings preserve named community knowledge without claiming to exhaust the Nation’s experience or establish every cause of change.

passages.title: Making strong, decorated baskets
passages.text: Fort Liard’s craft account describes selecting young, light-coloured spruce roots that bend without breaking easily. Long, straight roots reduce the number of joins needed in stitching. Their usefulness depends on choosing and preparing the material, not simply finding any root in the forest.

passages.title: Making strong, decorated baskets
passages.text: Makers split and peel the roots, soften them, and use flexible outer pieces for stitching. Prepared roots can be dried and moistened again when needed. This sequence turns a woodland material into a sewing element that can be stored and fitted to later work.

passages.title: Making strong, decorated baskets
passages.text: Birchbark basket making begins with a cut pattern and a prepared surface. Floral designs are laid out before damp quills are inserted through small awl holes. Decoration therefore forms part of a planned construction sequence, rather than an addition that can be placed anywhere without regard to the basket’s shape.

passages.title: Making strong, decorated baskets
passages.text: An inner bark lining, a sewn bottom and a split willow rim help form the container. A matching lid can be joined with moosehide strips. The published method includes sandpaper, a planer and clothespins, showing a living craft that combines inherited knowledge with available tools.

passages.title: Work, institutions and historical change
passages.text: The Fort Liard craft enterprise, founded in 1976, sells work made by producers in the community. Its range includes birchbark baskets, moccasins, mittens and mukluks. The business connects household skill with income and visitors, while its products combine older techniques with modern materials.

passages.title: Work, institutions and historical change
passages.text: The surviving Fort Liard treaty adhesion names Chief Thomas E. Kinla and two headmen alongside Commissioner Thomas William Harris. Dated 17 July 1922, it is a specific documentary trace of the encounter. Its existence does not mean that later disputes about land or the treaty’s meaning were resolved.

passages.title: Work, institutions and historical change
passages.text: The Nation’s wellness plan describes the lasting effects of infectious disease and residential or boarding schools. It also records continued harvesting and community action. These accounts place cultural survival alongside serious colonial losses, rather than presenting either disruption or continuity as the whole story.

passages.title: Work, institutions and historical change
passages.text: The 2024 plan proposes bringing Elders and young people together for sewing, hide tanning, tool making and community history. It also supports stories, language and land-based learning. These are stated priorities for passing knowledge on; the plan alone does not show that every proposed activity has already happened.

Acho Dene Koe continues as a First Nation with a living homeland and community institutions. Treaty and land negotiations concern rights and government, not the disappearance of the people. The map’s 1500 endpoint is imported coverage, not a historical fall date.

passages.text: Adal was a Muslim sultanate in the Horn of Africa, connected with the Gulf of Aden coast and the Harar plateau. Its principal centres included Dakar and later Harar. Cities and communities continued as political authority changed.

passages.title: An urban achievement
passages.text: Harar’s narrow lanes connect houses with a central concentration of religious and commercial buildings. Five historic gates corresponded to routes into the city and its neighbourhoods.

passages.title: An urban achievement
passages.text: Traditional Harari houses and their decorated interiors remain distinctive. Later Indian merchants introduced verandas, and builders combined the two traditions. Surviving houses therefore preserve several periods, not one Adal-era design.

passages.title: Food, animals and household work
passages.text: Excavations at Harar recovered cattle, goat and sheep bones, along with other animals. Cattle were the most frequent domestic species among identified fragments. These deposits span several centuries, so the sample cannot define a single meal or an exclusively Adal-era diet.

passages.title: Food, animals and household work
passages.text: Many cattle survived to adulthood, while goats at Harar were less often slaughtered young than those at the earlier town of Harlaa. Researchers interpret this as greater emphasis on maintaining herds. Bone ages reveal choices in animal management, rather than recipes.

passages.title: Food, animals and household work
passages.text: Harlaa’s excavated trade goods and imported marine fish should not simply be transferred to Harar’s story. Harar’s studied assemblages contained no fish bones and few luxury imports. Neighbouring towns had distinct histories and material economies.

passages.title: Discovering the city’s religious history
passages.text: Excavations at six mosques tested traditional foundation dates. The recovered radiocarbon evidence ranges from the late fifteenth to early twentieth centuries. It records different episodes of building and use, not six identical foundation dates.

passages.title: Discovering the city’s religious history
passages.text: At Din Agobera, a burial near the prayer niche supplied an early date range, from the late fifteenth to mid-seventeenth century. The excavators infer that the mosque was already present. The burial fill does not directly date its construction.

passages.title: Discovering the city’s religious history
passages.text: Later repairs changed Harar’s mosques substantially. At Din Agobera, a lighter corrugated roof replaced the heavy roof formerly supported by pillars. Older-looking buildings may contain materials and layouts from repeated rebuilding.

passages.title: Discovering the city’s religious history
passages.text: Aw Meshad’s teaching residence accommodated pupils studying the Quran, law and Arabic. Excavated drainage and floors belong to its later history, with dates in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. They cannot demonstrate an unchanged Adal-era school.

passages.title: Continuing knowledge and craft
passages.text: Harari weaving, basket making and bookbinding remain living crafts. Their continuity is part of the city’s heritage; it does not establish an Adal-era date for every surviving technique.

In the sixteenth century, military reverses, internal struggles and conflict accompanying Oromo movements weakened the sultanate. Its principal seat shifted toward Aussa, followed by separate Aussa and Harar polities. This political fragmentation did not end Harari urban life or the region’s Muslim communities.

passages.text: Aksum linked the northern Ethiopian highlands to the Red Sea through Adulis. Its monuments and inscriptions reveal a kingdom connected to African and Mediterranean exchange networks. The city also retained religious and ceremonial importance after its political power diminished.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Stoneworkers carved enormous stelae from single blocks. Some imitate multi-storey buildings, preserving an architectural vocabulary in stone.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The carved stelae belong especially to the third and fourth centuries CE. Royal tombs and later palace ruins reveal several phases of monumental construction.

passages.title: Writing and ideas
passages.text: King Ezana's fourth-century inscriptions used Greek, Sabaean and Ge'ez. Their multiple languages make connections across the region visible.

passages.title: Writing and ideas
passages.text: Christianity was introduced during the fourth century. Church building subsequently became part of the city's sacred landscape.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Adulis connected maritime commerce with inland routes, while ivory trade linked Aksum with Sudan.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Later Ethiopian emperors continued to be crowned at Aksum. Political decline did not erase its ceremonial role.

passages.text: The Almohads made Marrakesh a center of government and learning while maintaining a major Iberian center at Seville. Monumental mosques, gates and city walls gave their rule an enduring architectural presence.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Kutubiyya mosque and minaret formed a major landmark in Marrakesh. Walls and monumental gateways also shaped the imperial capital.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Almohad decoration emphasized organized geometric patterns and increasingly schematic ornament.

passages.title: Ideas and learning
passages.text: The courts at Marrakesh and Seville supported Islamic learning within a program of religious reform.

passages.title: Urban life
passages.text: Fez expanded under the Almohads, with the old city reaching the extent described by UNESCO as its present-day size.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Almohad Marrakesh remained a capital into the thirteenth century. Later dynasties inherited a city whose monuments continued to structure urban life.

passages.text: The Almoravids governed from Marrakesh and connected Saharan routes with North African and Iberian towns. Their rule supported major religious buildings and crafts, while their capital helped shape the urban geography of the western Islamic world.

passages.title: Technology and towns
passages.text: Marrakesh was an Almoravid foundation. Its palm grove is traditionally attributed to their period, linking the capital with a managed cultivated landscape.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Ali ibn Yusuf commissioned a richly worked mosque minbar in 1137. It later became associated with the Kutubiyya Mosque.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Textile manufacture in Almeria shows that Almoravid cultural production included luxurious fabrics as well as mosque building.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Almoravid power connected important ports with trans-Saharan commerce. The state's economy crossed both sea and desert.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Almohads replaced Almoravid rule in Marrakesh in the mid-twelfth century and retained the city as a capital.

passages.text: American Samoa is a United States territory in the eastern Samoan archipelago, with a cultural history much older than that political relationship. Basalt quarries, siapo barkcloth, schools and government records illuminate skilled work, community life and changing authority. Its history is connected with, but politically distinct from, the independent state of Samoa.

passages.title: Stoneworking and archaeological discovery
passages.text: Tutuila's Tataga-matau quarry above Leone formed part of a wider landscape of basalt extraction and tool making. Te Rangi Hiroa investigated it in 1927 with information from village elders. Quarry research combines physical remains with knowledge retained by local communities.

passages.title: Stoneworking and archaeological discovery
passages.text: A 2007 study analyzed geological samples from four Tutuila quarries and distinguished their chemical signatures. This supplies a way to test where a stone tool originated. It does not, by itself, date a tool or identify the person who carried it between islands.

passages.title: Siapo, makers and technical knowledge
passages.text: Hamilton Library in Hawaii holds a siapo mamanu made by Mary Pritchard around 1965, using mulberry bark and organic dyes. A named artist and a dated work make it possible to follow a particular contribution to Samoan art instead of treating every cloth as anonymous tradition.

passages.title: Siapo, makers and technical knowledge
passages.text: Siapo makers soften bark, scrape it with shells and beat it on a wooden anvil. Joining sheets creates larger surfaces for decoration. Pattern-board printing and freehand mamanu painting offer different ways to arrange designs, with hand finishing allowing variation between repeated forms.

passages.title: Siapo, makers and technical knowledge
passages.text: Pritchard recalled learning in Leone from Kolone Fai'ivae Leoso and other women while helping cultivate and harvest paper mulberry. Her account links artistic training to gardening, preparation, conversation and shared work, rather than only the final painted surface.

passages.title: Siapo, makers and technical knowledge
passages.text: Pritchard also described exporting siapo and adapting designs to shirts, dresses and household cloth. Those recollections show artists responding to markets while teaching and sustaining their practice. Innovation and cultural continuity could be parts of the same working life.

passages.title: Food, education and daily institutions
passages.text: An umu uses heated stones and layers of leaves to cook food for family gatherings. Taro, breadfruit, fish and other ingredients can share the cooking space. Preparing such a meal joins knowledge of heat, plant materials and timing with cooperative work.

passages.title: Food, education and daily institutions
passages.text: Palusami combines taro leaves with coconut cream, wrapped and cooked until tender. The dish makes two cultivated plants central to a shared meal, alongside other foods that vary with the household and occasion.

passages.title: Food, education and daily institutions
passages.text: Atauloma Girls School on Tutuila opened in 1900 through the London Missionary Society, with funds raised by Samoan residents. Classrooms and dormitories made formal schooling possible away from home, while its preparation of future pastors' wives reflected a particular religious and gendered purpose.

passages.title: Food, education and daily institutions
passages.text: The National Park Service's 1993 lease included village-owned land managed through the matai system. A later Traditional Use Study documented knowledge of plants, marine resources and culturally important places. Continuing local access is part of maintaining that knowledge.

passages.title: Reading political change through records
passages.text: The 1900 Tutuila and Aunu'u deed transferred sovereignty while promising protection of land and property and qualified retention of chiefly control of towns. Its clauses reveal which powers and protections were being negotiated; the document alone cannot represent every resident's view.

passages.title: Reading political change through records
passages.text: The Manu'a deed of 1904 was signed by Tuimanu'a and island chiefs. American Samoa's archives emphasize his annotation concerning equality and tradition. The territorial commission later stressed that US authority had already been proclaimed before the cessions, complicating a simple story of voluntary transfer.

passages.title: Reading political change through records
passages.text: President Truman's executive order transferred administration from the Navy to the Interior Department effective 1 July 1951. Voters first elected a governor in 1977. These changes concerned how the territory was governed, while Samoan family and village institutions continued.

American Samoa continues as a US territory. Naval government ended in 1951, and later constitutional and electoral changes expanded local political institutions. Those transitions did not end Samoan communities, language, chiefly relationships or artistic practice, nor did they unite the territory politically with independent Samoa.

passages.text: Asante architecture joined construction skill with visual language and religious practice. Surviving shrine buildings near Kumasi preserve parts of a tradition that remained meaningful beyond the period of imperial power.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Builders arranged timber and bamboo structures around courtyards, applying mud plaster to walls and originally roofing them with thatch.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Wall reliefs combine spirals with animal, bird and plant forms. Motifs related to Adinkra convey meanings as well as decorate surfaces.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Shrines are places for consultation with deities before important decisions. Their symbolic features belong to continuing religious practice.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Maintaining earthen buildings requires responding to heavy rain, humidity and damage to organic materials. Architectural survival depends on repeated care.

passages.text: Aboriginal peoples of Australia comprise many nations with their own languages, knowledge and relationships to Country. A continent-wide label cannot describe one kingdom or one way of life. The examples here come mainly from the mainland and identify particular places; Torres Strait Islander peoples have distinct histories.

passages.title: Food preparation preserved in stone
passages.text: At Madjedbebe in Mirarr Country, researchers examined grinding stones from deposits spanning the Ice Age and later periods. Wear patterns and chemical residues indicate processing of seeds and other plants. Two stones from the oldest occupation phase, GS39 and GS73, carry evidence interpreted as seed grinding.

passages.title: Food preparation preserved in stone
passages.text: A shaped sandstone whetstone, GS79, occurs in that early phase alongside an axe and flakes removed from ground tools. Together they support the interpretation that people made and maintained sharpened stone edges. Shape alone would be weaker evidence than this combination of objects and wear.

passages.title: Food preparation preserved in stone
passages.text: Red pigments on some stones also indicate grinding, but the researchers rejected many stains as contamination. Surviving pigment does not identify the images once painted, and preservation favours mineral traces over many food residues. An archaeological sample is therefore not a complete picture of daily activity.

passages.title: Engineering a wetland food supply
passages.text: At Budj Bim in south-western Victoria, Gunditjmara builders used volcanic stone to redirect water through channels, dams and weirs. These structures helped trap and hold short-finned eels. Their operation depended on knowledge of water flow and the animals’ seasonal movement.

passages.title: Engineering a wetland food supply
passages.text: Kurtonitj preserves stone house sites, eel traps, channels and trees used for smoking eels. These connected traces show a landscape of food production, processing and settlement. They are specific evidence from Gunditjmara Country, not a template for every Australian environment.

passages.title: Clothing, tools and exchange
passages.text: Wooden boomerangs recovered at Wyrie Swamp in South Australia in 1973 were dated to about 10,000 years ago. They demonstrate ancient woodworking, while their survival cannot establish when the first boomerang was invented. Most Australian boomerangs are not the returning form familiar from popular imagery.

passages.title: Clothing, tools and exchange
passages.text: Boomerangs served as hunting tools, digging implements and percussion instruments, with forms adapted to different tasks. Hooked examples from north-central Australia and heavy carved examples from the Darling and Cooper river systems travelled through exchange networks. Technique and decoration varied among makers and communities.

passages.title: Clothing, tools and exchange
passages.text: People in colder regions made clothing from animal skins. In Noongar language, kangaroo-skin cloaks are called booka. The museum also holds a 2005 reproduction by Lee Darroch and Treahna Hamm of a possum-skin cloak collected at Echuca in 1853, linking practical clothing to cultural renewal.

passages.title: Knowledge and community action
passages.text: Seasonal knowledge guides activities on Country. In recent collaborations, Indigenous knowledge holders and CSIRO have created calendars that communicate local environmental understanding. Ngan’gi, Walmajarri and Kunwinjku projects are distinct examples, not different versions of one national calendar.

passages.title: Knowledge and community action
passages.text: From 1792, Pemulwuy led resistance near the Parramatta, Hawkesbury and Georges rivers. His actions and the punitive colonial response show that occupation was contested. This Sydney-region history should not be assigned automatically to distant communities with different experiences of invasion.

passages.title: Knowledge and community action
passages.text: The 1967 campaign drew on petitions, community organising and alliances. Joe McGinness and Faith Bandler were among its leading organisers. The resulting constitutional change did not first grant voting rights: the federal franchise had already been extended in 1962.

Colonisation brought profound losses of land, lives and self-government, but Aboriginal peoples did not disappear. Communities continue in urban, regional and remote Australia, maintaining and renewing distinct identities. A change or ending in this broad map label records the atlas’s categories, not a single surrender or the end of a people.

passages.text: Ayutthaya, founded on an island in the Chao Phraya in 1351, ruled Siam for four centuries and was one of the great trading cities of Asia. Its kings took the Khmer idea of divine kingship, and its port welcomed Chinese, Japanese, Persian, Dutch, Portuguese and French merchants.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Rice, deer hides, sappanwood and tin left through the royal warehouses; Chinese junks and, from 1511, Portuguese ships came to buy them.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Foreign quarters ringed the city: Japanese, Portuguese, Dutch from 1608, French and Persian; the Greek Constantine Phaulkon rose to chief minister under King Narai.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: King Narai sent an embassy to Louis XIV at Versailles in 1686.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Prang towers in the Khmer manner and the tall chedis of Wat Phra Si Sanphet, with gilded Buddhas.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Court poetry, the Ramakien, the Thai Ramayana, and masked dance drama.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Theravada Buddhism with royal patronage and hundreds of temples in the capital.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Khmer court ritual and the devaraja idea of the king as a god shaped kingship; the law code of 1805 preserves Ayutthaya's laws.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Historic City of Ayutthaya was listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Thai kingship, law and court culture descend from Ayutthaya.
A Burmese army took and burned the city in April 1767. Within the year Taksin had rallied Siam from a new capital at Thonburi.

passages.text: Tenochtitlan brought canals, markets, workshops and ceremonial architecture into a large lake city. This card focuses on the capital's civic and artistic life within the Aztec imperial world.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Canals and raised causeways connected the capital to surrounding lakeshore towns. Canoes carried people and goods through the urban network.

passages.title: Water and daily life
passages.text: Aqueducts supplied fresh water, while neighborhood communities maintained local temples and markets.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Stone carvers used stone and hardwood tools, fiber cords, water and sand to shape even hard materials into detailed sculpture.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: The Templo Mayor paired shrines to Tlaloc and Huitzilopochtli. Successive rulers enlarged the complex, sometimes also responding to flooding and unstable ground.

passages.title: Craft and exchange
passages.text: The capital's markets offered food and luxury goods. Its neighborhoods included potters, weavers, sculptors, lapidaries and featherworkers.
Tenochtitlan fell in 1521. Spanish rulers built a new colonial capital over the devastated city.

passages.text: Baekje held the southwest of the Korean peninsula and was the most refined of the Three Kingdoms, trading by sea with China and Japan. Its monks, scholars and craftsmen carried Buddhism, Chinese learning and temple architecture to the Yamato court.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Sea routes linked Baekje to the southern Chinese dynasties and to Japan, and possibly further south.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: King Seong sent a Buddha image, sutras and monks to the Yamato court, the official introduction of Buddhism to Japan; Japanese sources date it to 538 or 552.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Baekje smile, the gentle expression of its stone and bronze Buddhas, as on the rock-cut triad at Seosan.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Gilt-bronze Buddhas, reliquaries and roof tiles stamped with lotus designs.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Gilt-bronze Incense Burner of Baekje, found at Neungsan-ri in 1993, a mountain of peaks, musicians and animals on a lotus base.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The monk Marananta arrived from Eastern Jin and the court adopted Buddhism, building temples and monastic communities.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Confucian learning and the Chinese classics were taught to the aristocracy; Baekje scholars such as Wang In took the classics to Japan.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Baekje Historic Areas were listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Baekje's transmission of Buddhism, writing and craft shaped early Japanese civilization.
A Silla army and a Tang fleet took the capital Sabi in 660; a restoration movement was crushed at the Baekgang river in 663, and Silla absorbed the land by 676.

passages.text: Balhae was founded in 698 by Dae Joyeong, a former Goguryeo general, in the hills of eastern Manchuria, and grew into a power that Tang writers called the Flourishing State of the East. Its capitals were laid out on the Tang model and its envoys sailed regularly to Japan.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Embassies went to Tang China and, more than thirty times, across the sea to Japan, carrying furs, ginseng and horses.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Balhae sat on the routes between Manchuria, the Korean peninsula, north China and the steppe.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Buddhism was practiced in the capitals, alongside the native beliefs of the Mohe majority.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: A Tang-style government of three chancelleries and six ministries ran a state of many peoples; the capital Sanggyeong copied the grid of Chang'an.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Korea, China and Russia each claim Balhae's story in their national histories.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Excavations of its walled capitals and tombs show a state that mixed Goguryeo, Mohe and Tang traditions.
The Khitan under Yelü Abaoji, founder of what became the Liao dynasty, took the capital Sanggyeong in 926 after a campaign of a few weeks. Refugees from the ruling class moved south into Goryeo.

passages.text: Benin's court commissioned brass sculpture to preserve royal memory and express authority. This Edo kingdom was centered in present-day Nigeria, distinct from the modern country named Benin.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: An incoming oba commissioned a commemorative head honoring his predecessor. These idealized royal images emphasize kingship rather than individual facial likeness.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Brass-casting guild artists produced rectangular plaques for the palace. A surviving example is dated approximately 1540 to 1570.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: Palace courtyards and galleries included wooden pillars covered with cast brass plaques.

passages.title: Historical memory
passages.text: Scholars interpret palace plaques as an archive later consulted about court ritual and regalia.

passages.title: Historical evidence
passages.text: British removal of royal works in 1897 disrupted their original contexts. Scholars therefore combine stylistic and material evidence when reconstructing their chronology.

passages.text: Buganda grew around the Kabaka, chiefs and clans in the Lake Victoria region. Its history can also be read in barkcloth workshops, the wooden architecture of Kasubi and recordings of court musicians. Royal government changed under colonial rule and was later abolished; Baganda cultural life and a restored royal institution continue.

passages.title: Buildings that preserve knowledge
passages.text: Kasubi's palace became a royal burial ground in 1884. The main building, Muzibu Azaala Mpanga, used a circular plan, a domed thatched roof and wooden supports. Monumental architecture here depended on skilled work with plant materials, rather than masonry.

passages.title: Buildings that preserve knowledge
passages.text: The documented interior combined palm-frond structural rings with long poles wrapped in barkcloth. A drum house and gatehouse faced the courtyard. These details connect construction, textile work and ceremonial movement within one royal compound.

passages.title: Buildings that preserve knowledge
passages.text: After the destructive 2010 fire, restoration drew on surviving building knowledge as well as documentation. Kasubi left UNESCO's danger list in 2023. Conservation work announced in 2026 addresses disaster preparation, site management and community participation.

passages.title: Barkcloth and household work
passages.text: Craftspeople harvest the Mutuba tree's inner bark in the wet season and beat it with wooden mallets. Working under an open shed keeps it from drying too quickly. Repeated skilled handling produces a soft sheet from bark, without weaving threads.

passages.title: Barkcloth and household work
passages.text: Barkcloth served as bedding, curtains, storage material and clothing as well as ceremonial dress. Its household uses place the craft within ordinary work and comfort, alongside the royal and funerary settings in which it remains especially visible.

passages.title: Barkcloth and household work
passages.text: UNESCO identifies Ngonge clan craftspeople and a hereditary chief craftsman as custodians of this knowledge. Imported cotton reduced demand during the nineteenth century. Continued ceremonial use and later promotion helped sustain skills through a changing textile economy.

passages.title: Listening to musicians across generations
passages.text: The 2021 album Buganda Royal Music Revival places archival sessions beside recordings made in 2017. Its credits name recordists and dates, allowing listeners to distinguish historical documentation from later performances rather than treating all tracks as one ancient sound.

passages.title: Listening to musicians across generations
passages.text: The collection includes the endongo lyre, the large akadinda xylophone and an entenga ensemble of tuned drums. These are different approaches to melody, resonance and ensemble coordination, not interchangeable examples of drumming.

passages.title: Listening to musicians across generations
passages.text: Performers credited include lyre player Albert Bisaso Ssempeke and royal harpist Temutewo Mukasa. Naming musicians preserves individual artistic work within a court tradition too often described only through kings and ceremonies.

passages.title: Councils and changing authority
passages.text: The Lukiiko developed from advisory councils of chiefs and clan heads. Its organization changed during the nineteenth century and under the 1900 agreement. Its present cultural and consultative role should not be projected unchanged onto earlier royal government.

passages.title: Councils and changing authority
passages.text: Article 118 of Uganda's 1967 constitution explicitly abolished royal offices. For Buganda it made that provision effective from 24 May 1966. This distinction explains why histories mention both years when describing the suppression of the kingdom.

Buganda's royal political institutions were suppressed during the 1966 crisis and the constitutional changes of 1967. Their restoration in 1993 established a cultural role within Uganda. Baganda communities, crafts and music continued across that interruption; the map's final snapshot is not their disappearance.

passages.text: Bunyoro in western Uganda connected royal institutions with farming, exchange and specialist production. At Kibiro, pottery and living salt-working practices reveal a history beyond royal genealogies. British conquest reshaped the kingdom; later abolition and cultural restoration of the monarchy are separate from the continuing lives of Banyoro communities.

passages.title: What Kibiro's archaeology reveals
passages.text: Excavations at Kibiro on Lake Albert uncovered abundant pottery associated with a salt-producing settlement. In his 1991 report, Graham Connah placed the origins of this important economic center early in the second millennium CE. This is evidence about a settlement and livelihood, not a secure founding date for Bunyoro.

passages.title: What Kibiro's archaeology reveals
passages.text: Many Kibiro pots carried patterns impressed with roulettes, including carved rollers. Connah interpreted these as connections toward the upper Nile or regions farther west. Similar decoration supports comparison and contact; it does not by itself identify the makers' language or ethnicity.

passages.title: What Kibiro's archaeology reveals
passages.text: Uganda's heritage submission identifies pottery used in leaching and boiling salt. Broken vessels therefore preserve traces of an industrial process as well as decorative choices. Its broad dates are less precise than a dated excavation context and should be used cautiously.

passages.title: Women's work and salt-making skill
passages.text: At Kibiro, workers spread and recycle earth over salt gardens so saline water rises into it. They collect the salty material, leach it and boil the resulting liquid to crystallize salt. The sequence combines knowledge of soil, water and heat.

passages.title: Women's work and salt-making skill
passages.text: Women carry out the salt work and inherit rights to garden plots through female relationships. These arrangements tie expertise to access to a productive place. Fishing complements salt production in the lakeshore economy.

passages.title: Women's work and salt-making skill
passages.text: Kibiro was proposed on Uganda's World Heritage Tentative List in 2025. That proposal documents a living workplace, not simply an abandoned ruin. Tentative status is distinct from inscription on the World Heritage List.

passages.title: Names, meals and social ties
passages.text: Empaako is an additional name used among Banyoro and neighboring communities. Addressing someone by this name can express affection and respect or ease tension. It identifies a relationship between people rather than merely distinguishing one individual from another.

passages.title: Names, meals and social ties
passages.text: In UNESCO's documented naming ceremony, paternal aunts consider the child's resemblance to relatives and the clan head announces the name. A meal of millet and smoked beef, gifts and a planted tree follow. Household ritual joins kinship with food and obligations of care.

passages.title: Names, meals and social ties
passages.text: The tradition entered UNESCO's Urgent Safeguarding List in 2013 because transmission and use of its associated language were weakening. Recognition concerns support for a living practice; it does not mean that the community or naming tradition had ended.

passages.title: Political change and its consequences
passages.text: The British-Buganda coalition defeated and deported Kabarega in 1899. Colonial incorporation and the transfer of territory changed the scale and authority of Bunyoro. These events concerned a political kingdom whose people and dynasty continued afterward.

passages.title: Political change and its consequences
passages.text: Historian G. N. Uzoigwe interprets Bunyoro's contraction through interacting causes: decisions by rulers, disease affecting people and animals, and violent British conquest. This is a historical argument about a long crisis, not evidence for one battle explaining every loss.

passages.title: Political change and its consequences
passages.text: In the 1964 referendum, voters in Buyaga and Bugangaizi chose a return to Bunyoro after their earlier transfer to Buganda under colonial rule. The vote shows that territorial change also involved local political choices, not only decisions made at royal courts.

Conquest in the late nineteenth century ended Bunyoro's independent political power. Uganda abolished kingship in 1967, and the monarchy returned with cultural functions in 1994. Banyoro communities and practices continued through those changes. Neither the salt village's age nor the map's last snapshot establishes a single lifetime for the kingdom.

passages.text: Caddo peoples built distinct river-valley communities linked by language, kinship and exchange. House traces, a surviving canoe and pottery reveal skilled work alongside farming and ceremonial life. Colonial dispossession forced major movements, but Caddo people continued and today sustain the Caddo Nation and renewed artistic traditions.

passages.title: Homes, hearths and travel
passages.text: At the George C. Davis site in east Texas, excavators found overlapping post patterns left by wooden buildings. Radiocarbon evidence places the main community between the ninth and early fourteenth centuries. Buildings were repeatedly renewed as people lived around ceremonial mounds.

passages.title: Homes, hearths and travel
passages.text: A magnetic survey detected structures invisible on the surface. Excavation in 2003 confirmed one large building with a central hearth and four internal roof supports. The pattern reveals engineering and interior space, although it does not identify every activity or occupant.

passages.title: Homes, hearths and travel
passages.text: A dugout canoe eroding from a Red River bluff in northwestern Louisiana was radiocarbon dated to about 1000 CE. The surviving wooden vessel gives direct evidence of water transport beyond later written descriptions.

passages.title: Food and shared work
passages.text: Late-seventeenth-century accounts describe corn stored in raised granaries, seed kept for planting and dried beans, squash and fruit. Storage helped households bridge seasonal shortages. These accounts mainly concern Hasinai communities and cannot describe every Caddo settlement.

passages.title: Food and shared work
passages.text: Housebuilding, planting and harvest brought people together. Maternal kinship connected households, while chiefs consulted community elders. Such relationships organized practical work as well as public decisions.

passages.title: Pottery as technology and art
passages.text: Caddo potters built vessels by joining coils of prepared clay to a base, then thinning and smoothing the walls. Temper mixed into clay and controlled drying helped a vessel survive manufacture and firing. Cooking pots and decorated bottles required different choices of shape and finish.

passages.title: Pottery as technology and art
passages.text: Engraved designs cut across a vessel's surface, unlike incised lines pressed into damp clay. Researchers and potters debate whether some ancient engraving occurred before or after firing. Modern experiments illuminate the skill without proving one method was universal.

passages.title: Pottery as technology and art
passages.text: Jereldine Redcorn's 1998 bottle Taysha has hollow tripod feet containing clay balls that rattle. Its form joins visual pattern with sound. It is a documented modern artwork drawing on ancestral pottery, not an excavated ancient vessel.

passages.title: Pottery as technology and art
passages.text: Redcorn learned through study, experiment and conversations with archaeologists when there was no local group of elder potters to teach her. Her work shows renewal as active investigation and artistic choice, not simply copying old designs.

passages.title: Dispossession and a continuing Nation
passages.text: The 1835 cession forced Caddo groups from lands in present Louisiana and Arkansas. Families moved toward Texas and, in some cases, Mexico. The agreement did not give them a secure replacement home.

passages.title: Dispossession and a continuing Nation
passages.text: In 1859, renewed pressure forced people from the Brazos reservation to Indian Territory. They left cultivated land and family graves behind. This was a rupture in community life, not the disappearance of Caddo people.

passages.title: Dispossession and a continuing Nation
passages.text: The Caddo Nation's education services include cultural learning and vocational support. These are contemporary institutions serving people with changing needs, alongside the continued importance of language, arts and family histories.

Caddo communities endured repeated dispossession, including the forced move of 1859. The Caddo Nation and Caddo cultural life continue. The end of an imported map interval is not an extinction date, and the many earlier communities should not be treated as a single kingdom with one fall.

passages.text: Cao Wei was the most powerful of the Three Kingdoms, controlling the northern heartland of China. Founded by Cao Cao's son Cao Pi, it inherited the Han administrative system and produced significant literary and military achievements.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Cao Cao and his sons Cao Pi and Cao Zhi wrote some of the finest poetry of the age, the Jian'an style named for the last Han reign period.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Cao Pi's Discourse on Literature, the first systematic essay of Chinese literary criticism, argues that writing outlasts rank and wealth.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Ma Jun builds a south-pointing chariot, a cart whose figure keeps pointing south as it turns, through gearing whose design is reconstructed with differential gears.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The tuntian system of military-agricultural colonies, begun by Cao Cao in 196 under the last Han emperor, settled soldiers and refugees on frontier land.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Administrative innovations passed to the Jin dynasty, among them the nine-rank system for grading officials, introduced in 220.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The fourteenth-century novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms later romanticized this era.
Sima Yan forced the last Wei emperor to abdicate and founded the Jin dynasty, in the last month of 265 by the Chinese calendar, February 266 by ours.

passages.text: Carolingian rulers made learning, Christian worship and patronage part of imperial government. Their workshops and scholars adapted older traditions into books, buildings and objects that influenced medieval Europe.

passages.title: Writing
passages.text: The drive for accurate, readable texts encouraged Carolingian minuscule, a clear script based on Roman letter forms.

passages.title: Learning
passages.text: Charlemagne gathered scholars including Alcuin, Theodulf and Paul the Lombard. Court patronage supported educational and liturgical reform.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Illuminated books and carved ivory panels combined classical figures with local ornamental traditions. Precious bindings could include gems and pearls.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: The palace chapel at Aachen has an octagonal core, an encircling aisle, upper galleries and a dome. Its antique columns were probably brought from Rome and Ravenna.

passages.title: Ideas and institutions
passages.text: Charlemagne received the imperial crown in Rome in 800. The ceremony tied royal authority to a Christian interpretation of Roman imperial tradition.

passages.title: Change and continuity
passages.text: Carolingian art continued after Charlemagne's death and political fragmentation. The end of a unified realm did not end its workshops or manuscript traditions.

passages.text: Carthage grew on the Gulf of Tunis into a major center of Punic civilization and Mediterranean commerce. Its ports connected communities, goods and artistic traditions. This card concerns the Punic city and its power before Roman destruction, rather than the later Roman city built on the same site.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The surviving Punic harbor remains make maritime infrastructure central to understanding Carthage's commercial power.

passages.title: Arts and beliefs
passages.text: Stelae from the sacred tophet show varied cultural influences. The imagery is evidence of artistic exchange as well as religious practice.

passages.title: Knowledge
passages.text: Magon was remembered as an agronomist and Hannon as a navigator. Agriculture and seafaring both belonged to Carthage's intellectual legacy.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Later Roman buildings at Carthage belong to a refounded city. They should not be attributed automatically to Punic builders.
Rome destroyed Punic Carthage in 146 BCE. A Roman city was later established on the site.

passages.text: Champa was a string of Cham kingdoms along the coast of what is now central Vietnam, first recorded by the Chinese as Lin-yi in 192 CE. Seafarers and traders, the Chams built brick towers to Shiva and fought the Khmer and the Vietnamese for more than a thousand years.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Brick tower temples at My Son, built from the seventh to the thirteenth century, with sandstone carving of a fineness that rivals Angkor.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Sandstone images of Shiva, Vishnu, Ganesha and dancing apsaras in the Cham styles of Tra Kieu and Dong Duong.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Cham ports sold agarwood, ivory, gold and cinnamon to China and the archipelago and sheltered ships waiting for the monsoon.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Cham sailors traded and raided across the South China Sea and up the Mekong; they sacked Angkor in 1177.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Shaivism was the royal cult, with Buddhism strong at Dong Duong in the ninth century; Islam reached the Chams from the fifteenth century.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Sanskrit and Cham inscriptions record kings and gifts to temples; the Dong Yen Chau stone of the fourth century is the oldest text in any Southeast Asian language.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: My Son Sanctuary was listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Cham communities in Vietnam and Cambodia keep the language and, in Cambodia, Islam.
The Vietnamese took the capital Vijaya in 1471; the last Cham principality, Panduranga, was absorbed by the Nguyen emperor Minh Mang in 1832.

sectionTitles: A writing system becomes a printed public voice

passages.text: Cherokee history includes distinct southeastern communities and continuing nations in Oklahoma and North Carolina. Writing, newspapers, basketry and food knowledge record achievements made by individuals and families as well as governments. Forced removal devastated communities, but Cherokee people rebuilt institutions and maintained connections to their homelands.

passages.title: A writing system becomes a printed public voice
passages.text: Sequoyah developed a syllabary for writing Cherokee. In 1825 the Nation commissioned English and Cherokee type for a press. Adapting a writing system to movable type connected linguistic invention with practical publishing equipment and organization.

passages.title: A writing system becomes a printed public voice
passages.text: The first Cherokee Phoenix appeared at New Echota on 21 February 1828. Its Cherokee and English columns made the same newspaper accessible across languages. Surviving issues are material evidence of Cherokee authorship and political communication before removal.

passages.title: A writing system becomes a printed public voice
passages.text: Publication continued in a new setting with the Cherokee Advocate, established in Tahlequah in 1844. It printed both languages as the Nation rebuilt schools, homes, businesses and government buildings after removal.

passages.title: Baskets, materials and teaching
passages.text: A rivercane basket from the Qualla Boundary, catalogued as 15/8659, was collected in 1927 or 1928. The museum records its twill-plaited construction but does not name its maker. The collection date should not be mistaken for the year it was woven.

passages.title: Baskets, materials and teaching
passages.text: Lottie Queen Stamper recalled her family making white-oak baskets after work in the fields. Preparing splints required carefully splitting wood into usable strips. Her recollection connects an admired finished object to seasonal farm work and demanding preparation.

passages.title: Baskets, materials and teaching
passages.text: Stamper expanded into rivercane and plant dyes, then recorded patterns in notebooks and on graph paper for students. Teaching changed how designs circulated between families and materials while preserving close attention to technique.

passages.title: Baskets, materials and teaching
passages.text: In 1940, Stamper studied a photograph of an older double-weave basket held in Britain and worked out its pattern. Other Cherokee elders still knew this technique. Her achievement strengthened its teaching; describing her as the sole rediscoverer would erase those weavers.

passages.title: Food, language and family knowledge
passages.text: Eastern Cherokee speaker Tommy Cabe describes gathering sochan greens with relatives in spring and later teaching his own children. His account includes care for the plant and gratitude before picking. It documents one living family tradition in its own voice.

passages.title: Food, language and family knowledge
passages.text: Cherokee Nation offers immersion education in Tahlequah, online teaching and a master-apprentice language program. Different ways of learning connect children and adults with speakers, continuing the language beyond what any historic printed page can preserve.

passages.title: Displacement, government and continuity
passages.text: In May 1838, federal troops and state militias began forcing Cherokee families into detention. People often had little time to collect possessions. Subsequent travel by roads and waterways brought further hardship, illness and death.

passages.title: Displacement, government and continuity
passages.text: The 1839 constitution was part of rebuilding, but it did not immediately resolve conflicts between earlier western migrants, removal supporters and those forced west. A new government should not be mistaken for an uncomplicated recovery from dispossession.

passages.title: Displacement, government and continuity
passages.text: Cherokee Nation and the United Keetoowah Band are based in Oklahoma; the Eastern Band is based in North Carolina. Each has its own government and citizenship system. The broad label Cherokee on this map includes histories that need these distinctions.

United States removal policies caused enormous loss of life, homes and land. They did not end Cherokee peoples or political life. Cherokee Nation, the United Keetoowah Band and the Eastern Band continue as distinct nations; the map's eighteenth-century endpoint describes only its available historical coverage.

passages.text: The Chimu kingdom made Chan Chan a major center on Peru's north coast. Its earthen compounds, craft production and water systems show how a large city organized resources in a dry coastal environment.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Canals and irrigation supported agriculture around Chan Chan. Roads helped connect the kingdom along the northern coast.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: Large walled compounds contained open courts, temples, dwellings, storage spaces, reservoirs and funerary platforms.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Earthen walls carried relief decoration with abstract patterns and human or animal subjects.

passages.title: Craft and work
passages.text: Specialized production areas supported weaving, woodworking and metalworking. These activities were part of the city's planned fabric.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Storage and water-management installations supported the city alongside agricultural land beyond its monumental center.

passages.title: Change over time
passages.text: The kingdom reached its height in the fifteenth century before incorporation into the Inca Empire. The source used here does not establish a precise conquest year.

passages.text: The Cholas of the Kaveri delta, restored under Vijayalaya in 848, ruled the Tamil south for four centuries and sent fleets across the Bay of Bengal. Their bronze Natarajas, the great temples of Thanjavur and Gangaikonda Cholapuram and their village assemblies are the high point of Tamil civilization.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Rajaraja I finished the Brihadisvara temple at Thanjavur, its granite tower about 66 meters high.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bronze images of Shiva Nataraja, cast by the lost-wax method, reached their classic form in the tenth and eleventh centuries.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Rajendra I sent a fleet against Srivijaya in 1025 and sacked its ports along the Strait of Malacca.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Merchant guilds such as the Ayyavole Five Hundred traded across the Indian Ocean, and Chola embassies reached Song China in 1015 and 1077.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Tanks, sluices and the Kaveri's old anicuts irrigated the delta's rice fields.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Ocean-going ships carried armies to Sri Lanka, the Maldives and Sumatra.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Village assemblies chose their committees by lot from eligible landholders, as the Uttaramerur inscriptions of the 920s record.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Great Living Chola Temples were listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Chola bronzes and temple styles were carried to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.
The Pandyas of Madurai defeated the Cholas repeatedly from the 1210s and absorbed the last of the kingdom by 1279.
