passages.text: Samoa has a long history of Pacific voyaging, skilled craft and family-based social institutions. This card follows the western islands through colonial government and independence, with clearly identified earlier background. Samoan people and culture also extend to American Samoa and overseas communities; the modern state is not the whole Samoan world.

passages.title: Discoveries and the deeper past
passages.text: Pottery fragments recovered during construction of the Mulifanua ferry berth on Upolu in 1973 included the tooth-stamped decoration associated with Lapita. Their context links the islands to a much older Pacific settlement history, long before the modern state.

passages.title: Discoveries and the deeper past
passages.text: A 2001 radiocarbon study placed occupation of the Mulifanua site around 930 to 800 BCE. These are calibrated estimates for a particular archaeological site, not an exact founding date for Samoa or a date assigned from a later genealogy.

passages.title: Craft knowledge and achievement
passages.text: A Samoan tattooing implement in Te Papa combines a bone comb, turtle-shell plate and wooden handle. A mallet drives the toothed edge, while combs of different widths make broad areas or fine lines. The object makes the precision of the tattooist's craft visible.

passages.title: Craft knowledge and achievement
passages.text: Ie Samoa fine mats are woven from narrow pandanus strips and finished with feathers and fringe. Preparing and weaving such fine material takes sustained skill and labor; the mats are valued for workmanship and the histories they acquire through exchange.

passages.title: Craft knowledge and achievement
passages.text: Fine mats circulate at weddings, funerals and other gatherings, reaffirming relationships between families. Village committees and master weavers teach the practice, making production a form of shared knowledge as well as individual artistry.

passages.title: Daily life and social obligations
passages.text: The aiga, or extended family, connects daily life with service, respect and reciprocal care. Family members exchange food, money and practical support, including across national borders. These obligations are lived and debated differently by different generations.

passages.title: Daily life and social obligations
passages.text: Matai titles, genealogies, language and ceremonial responsibilities are parts of fa'asamoa. Together they organize belonging and public relationships; the term does not describe an identical way of life for every Samoan household.

passages.title: Daily life and social obligations
passages.text: Christian teaching introduced by John Williams in 1830 became part of a changing religious landscape. Samoan forms of church life developed in close relationship with fa'asamoa, rather than simply replacing every earlier social institution.

passages.title: Colonial rule and political agency
passages.text: The arrival of the influenza-infected Talune in 1918 led to a devastating epidemic under New Zealand administration. The disaster affected families and food production, making colonial governance part of everyday experience as well as constitutional history.

passages.title: Colonial rule and political agency
passages.text: The Mau pursued self-government through organized, nonviolent resistance. In December 1929, colonial police killed peaceful demonstrators, including Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III. The movement's history records Samoan political action, not merely a transfer between foreign rulers.

passages.title: Colonial rule and political agency
passages.text: In 1936 New Zealand recognized the Mau as a legitimate political organization and repealed the Samoan Offenders Ordinance. Independence still required a longer struggle and arrived on 1 January 1962.

passages.title: Language and continuity
passages.text: Samoan language nests and school programs in New Zealand connect language learning with shared leadership and cultural knowledge. These institutions show how communities maintain and reshape connections to Samoa across generations of migration.

Colonial administration of Western Samoa ended with independence on 1 January 1962. Samoan communities, chiefly institutions and cultural practices continue in the independent state, American Samoa and the diaspora. A last map observation is not the end of the people or their history.

passages.text: The Great Seljuk Empire, founded when Tughril took Nishapur in 1037, brought Oghuz Turkic rule to Iran, Iraq and Anatolia under a Persian administration. Its sultans protected the Abbasid caliphs, built madrasas and mosques, and opened Anatolia to the Turks.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The vizier Nizam al-Mulk and his rival Taj al-Mulk added the two great brick domes to the Friday Mosque of Isfahan in 1086 and 1088.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Persian poetry, calligraphy and lustre ceramics flourished under Seljuk patronage; Omar Khayyam wrote the quatrains later gathered as the Rubaiyat.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Nizam al-Mulk founded the Nizamiyya of Baghdad, first of a network of madrasas teaching Shafi'i law and theology.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Alp Arslan's victory over the Byzantines at Manzikert opened Anatolia to Turkic settlement.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Nizam al-Mulk's Book of Government set out the Persian art of kingship for the sultans.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: The Jalali calendar, computed by Omar Khayyam and colleagues for Malik Shah, fixed the year to the spring equinox with an error of about one day in 3,770 years, less than the Gregorian calendar's.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Khayyam's treatise on algebra classified cubic equations and solved them with conic sections.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Turkic settlement of Anatolia that followed Manzikert led to the Sultanate of Rum and, in time, the Ottomans.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The madrasa became the standard school of Sunni learning.

After Malik Shah's death in 1092 the empire split among his heirs and their atabegs. The last sultan of Iraq, Tughril III, was killed in 1194 by the Khwarazmshah Tekish, who took Iran; the Seljuks of Rum in Anatolia lasted until 1308.

passages.text: This card concerns medieval Serbian principalities, the Nemanjic kingdom and empire, and later successor lordships. Their borders and institutions changed over time. Quarry settlements, burnt food, fish bones, illuminated books and a seal-maker's tool reveal work and learning beyond royal campaigns. Evidence from a monastery or court describes that setting, not every household.

passages.title: Building, labour and painted spaces
passages.text: Near Studenica, marble quarries and remains of a workers' settlement connect the Church of the Virgin with the people who extracted and shaped its stone. The monastery's finely finished surfaces depended on a wider landscape of skilled and demanding labour.

passages.title: Building, labour and painted spaces
passages.text: Studenica's Church of the Virgin combines a domed interior with an exterior drawing on Romanesque architecture. Its design became a model for other monasteries. Builders adapted forms circulating across the Adriatic and Byzantine worlds rather than working within a sealed national tradition.

passages.title: Building, labour and painted spaces
passages.text: Paintings made in the Church of the Virgin in 1208 and 1209 organise religious figures through expressive gestures and carefully conceived space. Their surviving setting lets historians study images as part of a building used for worship, rather than as detached museum pictures.

passages.title: Food recovered from the ground
passages.text: Charred remains from twelfth- and thirteenth-century buildings at Ras include bread wheat, rye, barley, oats and millet. Wheat was most abundant in the studied samples. Weeds mixed with grain, including corncockle, preserve traces of crop handling as well as the crops themselves.

passages.title: Food recovered from the ground
passages.text: The Ras study also identified a round piece of burnt bread, cereal remains in a pot and fragments of peach stones. These finds bring prepared food and fruit into view. They document particular deposits, not a complete menu or the quantities eaten by every resident.

passages.title: Food recovered from the ground
passages.text: Waste deposits at Studenica from the fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries contained catfish, carp and pike alongside migratory sturgeon. The researchers connect the sturgeon with the distant Danube. Feeding a monastery could involve both nearby fishing and longer supply routes.

passages.title: Food recovered from the ground
passages.text: Studenica's fish bones preserve information about body parts, size and cutting. The authors suggest that some large fish arrived whole, perhaps dried or salted. Preservation methods are an interpretation of the remains; the bones do not supply a surviving recipe.

passages.title: Mining towns and the tools of authority
passages.text: Excavation at Drenje in Rudnik revealed secular buildings and three churches, two Orthodox and one Catholic, in a settlement flourishing during the fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries. These remains suggest a varied religious landscape. Identifying the area specifically as the medieval market remains an interpretation.

passages.title: Mining towns and the tools of authority
passages.text: A seal-die from a pit at Rudnik bears Prince Lazar's name and a helmet with horned ornament. Dated to his rule there between 1373 and 1389, it is a tool for producing official impressions. No matching impression was known to the study's authors.

passages.title: Books, textiles and a riverside capital
passages.text: The late twelfth-century Miroslav Gospel combines writing on parchment with gilding and painted decoration. Its illuminations draw on Italian and Byzantine artistic traditions. The manuscript shows bookmaking as a collaboration of textual, material and visual skills shaped by connections beyond one court.

passages.title: Books, textiles and a riverside capital
passages.text: The Miroslav Gospel arranges readings for liturgical use rather than simply presenting an unbroken narrative. Its language and spelling also preserve evidence of a regional scribal tradition. A book could guide repeated communal worship while carrying the choices of the people who copied it.

passages.title: Books, textiles and a riverside capital
passages.text: An embroidered priestly stole, or epitrachelion, from the Church of Saints Peter and Paul near Novi Pazar preserves another demanding craft. The National Museum dates its style to the late fourteenth or early fifteenth century. This ceremonial garment cannot stand for ordinary clothing.

passages.title: Books, textiles and a riverside capital
passages.text: Smederevo's new court was built at the meeting of the Danube and Jezava in 1428 to 1430. Its builders faced shortages of local stone, bringing material from farther away and reusing older masonry. The fortress records transport and salvage as well as defensive planning.

Ottoman conquest of Smederevo in 1459 ended the remaining Serbian despotate. The medieval empire had fragmented much earlier; 1389 was not the date when all Serbian political institutions vanished. Settlement at Smederevo and religious communities such as Studenica continued under changed conditions. The imported map endpoint of 1300 is not a historical fall date.

passages.text: The Shang is the first Chinese dynasty confirmed by contemporary written records, surviving on oracle bones and bronze inscriptions. Centered in the Anyang region, it controlled a network of towns and dependent settlements through ritual authority and bronze technology.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: Oracle bone script, the direct ancestor of modern Chinese characters, carved on turtle plastrons and cattle shoulder blades to record the king's divinations. The earliest inscriptions date from the reign of Wu Ding.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: Horse-drawn chariots appear in Shang burials at Anyang, adopted from the steppe, and are used for hunting, display and war.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Piece-mold bronze casting reaches its peak. The Houmuwu ding from Anyang, the heaviest bronze vessel known from the ancient world, weighs 832 kg.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: A ten-day week and the sixty-day cycle of ten stems and twelve branches, still used in the Chinese calendar, organized Shang time; oracle bones are dated by the cycle.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Taotie masks and dragon motifs on bronze vessels show sophisticated design principles.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Jade carvings, marble sculptures and pottery figurines from royal tombs; the undisturbed tomb of Fu Hao, a consort of Wu Ding, held 755 jades and 468 bronzes.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Musical instruments including bronze bells and stone chimes found in Anyang excavations.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The supreme deity Di ruled over lesser spirits and royal ancestors who mediated between heaven and earth.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Royal divination addressed questions of war, harvest, weather, illness and the king's activities.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Human sacrifice accompanied royal burials, with dozens or hundreds of victims in major tombs.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Millet farming, with rice and wheat as lesser crops, supported urban populations at Anyang and other centers.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Silk production, evident from the impressions of silk wrappings preserved on bronze vessels.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The king hunted from chariots with bows and bronze-tipped arrows.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Cowrie shells from the Indian Ocean, given by the king as rewards and buried with the dead as wealth.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Tin and copper for bronze imported from distant sources.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Chinese writing system preserved in continuous use to the present day.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Bronze ritual vessel forms influenced Chinese metalwork for two thousand years.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The concept of a central royal authority over subordinate territories took root.
King Wu of Zhou defeated the last Shang king, Di Xin, at the Battle of Muye, ending the dynasty.

passages.text: Shu Han claimed legitimacy as the true successor to the Han dynasty, ruling Sichuan under Liu Bei and his famous chancellor Zhuge Liang. Though the smallest of the Three Kingdoms, it became the most romanticized in later literature.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The repeating crossbow, known since the Warring States, was improved under Zhuge Liang by tradition, along with the wooden ox, a wheelbarrow-like cart for carrying supplies over mountain roads.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Sichuan's irrigation, built around the Dujiangyan works of the third century BCE, was kept up and extended to feed the state.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Confucian legitimacy theory justified resistance to Cao Wei.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Loyalty and righteousness became central virtues in Shu Han ideology.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Zhuge Liang became the archetype of the brilliant but tragic loyal minister in Chinese culture.
Cao Wei general Deng Ai led a surprise attack through mountain passes and captured Chengdu, forcing Liu Shan to surrender.

passages.text: Silla began as the smallest of Korea's Three Kingdoms, in the southeast around Gyeongju, and by 676 had brought most of the peninsula under one rule. Its bone-rank aristocracy, gold crowns, Hwarang youth bands and Buddhist temples made a distinctive civilization that lasted nearly a thousand years.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Gold crowns with tree and antler uprights, hung with jade and gold spangles, from the royal mound tombs of Gyeongju.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bulguksa temple and the Seokguram grotto, with its granite Buddha facing the sea, were begun; UNESCO listed both in 1995.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Cheomseongdae, a stone tower built in the reign of Queen Seondeok (632 to 647), is among the oldest surviving astronomical observatories in the world.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The bone-rank system fixed a person's rank, office and even the size of their house by birth.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Hwarang, bands of aristocratic youths, trained in arms, song and Buddhist and Confucian teaching, and led Silla's armies.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Buddhism became the state religion after the martyrdom of Ichadon, and temples rose across the kingdom.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Gyeongju grew into a planned capital of palaces, temples, markets and tiled houses, with the Anapji pleasure pond laid out in 674.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Court culture prized refinement, poetry in the hyangga form and Buddhist devotion.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Gyeongju Historic Areas were listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Unified Silla's administration, Buddhism and script laid the foundations of later Korean culture.
The last king, Gyeongsun, surrendered to Goryeo in 935, ending nearly a millennium of Silla rule counted from its traditional founding in 57 BCE.

passages.text: Solomon Islands includes communities with distinct languages, artistic practices and island histories. Canoe ornaments, feather currency, shellwork and recordings reveal how people made useful objects, exchanged goods and performed together. Independence in 1978 began a new political chapter within much older and continuing cultural histories.

passages.title: Canoes, carving and skilled materials
passages.text: A late nineteenth- or early twentieth-century nguzunguzu at the Metropolitan Museum combines blackened wood with nautilus-shell inlay. The collection tentatively attributes it to New Georgia. Its carved face and hands show the close relationship between boat decoration, bodily ornament and spiritual protection.

passages.title: Canoes, carving and skilled materials
passages.text: Such figures were lashed near the base of a canoe's prow rather than carved as a permanent part of the hull. They could be removed, exchanged or transferred between boats. Canoes supported fishing and transport as well as warfare, so their making joined practical skill with ceremonial importance.

passages.title: Canoes, carving and skilled materials
passages.text: The names and interpretations of canoe figures vary between western island communities. Modern artists continue to use their forms as cultural and national symbols. A museum example can illuminate one tradition without representing every community in the country.

passages.title: Feather currency and exchange
passages.text: Te Papa holds a twentieth-century tevau collected on Peleni in the Santa Cruz Islands in 1969. Specialists attached small red feathers to overlapping platelets and decorated the coil with shell and fiber. Leaves and oilcloth protected this particular example during storage and travel.

passages.title: Feather currency and exchange
passages.text: Tevau could be exchanged for goods and services, including canoes, crops and pigs, and given in marriage ceremonies. Their value reflected color, condition and skilled labor; fading feathers could reduce it. This was a regional system of valuables, not a single currency used uniformly across all the islands.

passages.title: Shellwork and everyday connections
passages.text: In her fieldwork account of Baegu communities on Malaita, Kay Ross described ornaments made from small red, white and black shell discs. Plant fiber joined discs into planned geometric arrangements for belts and armbands. Fine finishing could make both sides presentable.

passages.title: Shellwork and everyday connections
passages.text: Ross also described coastal and inland communities exchanging fish and taro. Shell valuables circulated at weddings and feasts, where relatives helped assemble gifts. Her account records particular communities and a particular period, rather than a timeless rule for all Solomon Islanders.

passages.title: Music preserved in recordings
passages.text: Hugo Zemp's recordings of Fataleka and Baegu music, released in 1973, document bamboo panpipes, clapping sticks, singing and dance. Performances place instruments within funeral and other ceremonial settings, allowing listeners to hear coordination between people as well as individual sounds.

passages.title: Music preserved in recordings
passages.text: The album identifies Afunakwa as the singer of the lullaby Rorogwela. Other tracks feature women and girls singing or performers playing bamboo instruments. Named performers and recorded contexts help keep an account of music connected to people rather than an anonymous national style.

passages.title: Political change and continuing communities
passages.text: Internal self-government began on 2 January 1976, followed by constitutional negotiations in London in 1977. Debate included regional finances and the place of the Western Solomons in the new country. Independence emerged through negotiation and disagreement, not a universally shared timetable.

passages.title: Political change and continuing communities
passages.text: The Independence Order names 7 July 1978 as the appointed day. That document provides a precise date for the political transition, while art objects and recordings document cultural work that both preceded independence and continued afterward.

British protectorate rule ended with independence on 7 July 1978. Solomon Islands continues as a country whose communities have varied histories, languages and traditions. The political transition did not end regional identities, exchange relationships or creative practice.

passages.text: The Song dynasty oversaw an economic and technological revolution in China, though military weakness led to the loss of northern China in 1127. Printing, gunpowder, the compass and paper money transformed society, while Neo-Confucianism shaped intellectual life.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: Bi Sheng invents movable type printing, though woodblock remained more common.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: The first gunpowder formulas for military use appear in the Wujing Zongyao military manual.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: Shen Kuo describes the magnetic compass for navigation in his Dream Pool Essays.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Paper money, the jiaozi, issued by the government to facilitate commerce, the first state paper currency.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Early-ripening Champa rice from Vietnam is distributed to farmers, allowing two harvests a year in the south.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Landscape painting reaches its peak with masters like Fan Kuan and Guo Xi.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Porcelain production perfects celadon and qingbai wares.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Zhu Xi (1130 to 1200) synthesizes Neo-Confucianism; his commentaries on the Four Books, completed about 1190, became the examination curriculum for six centuries.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Maritime trade with Southeast Asia, India and the Middle East expands dramatically.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Porcelain exported throughout Asia and eventually to the Middle East and Africa.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Song technological innovations transformed the world when transmitted to Europe.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Neo-Confucianism became the dominant ideology in East Asia until the nineteenth century.
The Mongol conquest was completed when the last Song emperor drowned at the fall of the final Song stronghold at Yamen in 1279; Kublai Khan ruled China as the Yuan dynasty.

passages.text: Songhai's wealth linked Gao and the Niger region to trans-Saharan commerce. Its surviving monuments make construction, religious practice and shared maintenance visible alongside the better-known history of its rulers.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: At Gao, the Tomb of Askia combines an earthen pyramidal tower with mosque buildings, a cemetery and an assembly space.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Projecting wooden supports form permanent scaffolding. Renewing rain-eroded plaster is part of the building's continuing life.

passages.title: Learning
passages.text: During the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, Timbuktu was a center of Islamic learning and manuscript exchange.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Timbuktu's market brought together manuscripts, salt, gold, cattle and grain. Scholarship existed within a busy commercial city.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The mosques of Djingareyber, Sankore and Sidi Yahia preserve an earthen architectural tradition shaped by successive restorations.

passages.text: Architecture and painting show different sides of Spain's sixteenth- and seventeenth-century culture: a royal monastery organized around worship and learning, and pictures shaped by observation and international exchange.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Philip II founded El Escorial in 1563. Juan Bautista de Toledo designed the complex, and Juan de Herrera completed the work after Toledo's death.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: El Escorial combined a monastery, church, palace, school, seminary and royal library around courtyards. Religious life, royal authority and study occupied one complex.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Early in his seventeenth-century career, Velazquez painted kitchen scenes known as bodegones and studied figures directly from life.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Velazquez became painter to Philip IV in 1623. Later at Madrid, Venetian paintings and contact with Rubens helped shape his art.

passages.text: Srivijaya, a Malay kingdom based at Palembang on Sumatra from the seventh century, controlled the Strait of Malacca and the trade between India and China. Its rulers were patrons of Buddhism, and Old Malay, the language of its inscriptions, became the lingua franca of the archipelago.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The kingdom taxed ships passing the strait and made its ports the entrepot of the sea route between India and China.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Camphor, resins, gold, tin and spices went out; Chinese and Indian goods came in.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Missions to the Tang and Song courts kept the China trade open, and Arab writers knew the maharaja of Zabaj as lord of the islands.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Chinese monk Yijing stopped at Srivijaya in 671 and found more than a thousand monks; he advised pilgrims to study Sanskrit there before going on to India.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Kedukan Bukit inscription of 683, in Old Malay, is the oldest dated text in the language.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Mahayana Buddhism had royal patronage; the scholar Atisha studied at Srivijaya for twelve years before carrying its teaching to Tibet.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Malay spread as the trading language of the region and is the root of modern Malay and Indonesian.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The pattern of a port kingdom ruling the strait passed to Malacca.
The Cholas sacked the ports in 1025, Malayu at Jambi took the lead, and Javanese Singhasari and Majapahit pressed on Sumatra; Majapahit's attack on Palembang in 1377 ended the old kingdom.

passages.text: The Sui dynasty reunited China after three centuries of division, creating institutions that the Tang would inherit and perfect. Its ambitious building projects and military campaigns exhausted the state, leading to its rapid collapse.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Grand Canal's main sections are dug between 605 and 610, connecting the Yellow River and Yangzi River systems for grain transport.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Standardization of coinage, weights and measures across the reunified empire.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Buddhism receives imperial patronage; Emperor Wen styled himself a Buddhist universal monarch.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Civil service examinations begin, recruiting officials by Confucian learning; the jinshi degree dates from about 605.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Grand Canal remained China's main north-south transport artery for over a thousand years.
Emperor Yang's disastrous Korean campaigns and excessive building projects led to widespread rebellion; he was assassinated by his own guards in 618.

passages.text: Sukhothai, which broke from Khmer rule about 1238, is remembered as the first Thai kingdom. Its inscription of Ram Khamhaeng describes a father-king, its sculptors made the walking Buddha, and its script became the Thai alphabet.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: The Ram Khamhaeng inscription, dated 1283, says the king devised the Thai script from Khmer models; some scholars date the stone itself to the fifteenth century.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The walking Buddha, a figure in motion cast in bronze, is Sukhothai's own creation.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Lotus-bud chedis at Wat Mahathat and Sri Lankan-style bell stupas; glazed Sawankhalok stoneware was exported across the region.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Theravada Buddhism of the Sri Lankan school, brought by monks from Nakhon Si Thammarat, became the state religion.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The inscription describes a king who hears any subject's grievance when they ring the bell at the palace gate.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Historic Town of Sukhothai and Associated Historic Towns were listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Thai alphabet descends from the Sukhothai script.
Ayutthaya reduced Sukhothai to a vassal in 1378 and, when its royal line ended in 1438, made it a province.

passages.text: Early-modern Sweden supported both industrial communities and elaborate court art. Falun's copper landscape and Drottningholm's theatre reveal very different kinds of skilled work.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: In the seventeenth century, Falun copper production helped make Sweden a major European metal producer. Mining shaped the surrounding economy and settlement landscape.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Falun's seventeenth-century planned town and mining settlements preserve evidence of workers' housing as well as production facilities. Industrial history includes the communities around the mine.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Drottningholm's eighteenth-century theatre used machinery that could change scenery while the curtain stayed up. Stage sets and working mechanisms survive.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Drottningholm's Chinese Pavilion reflects eighteenth-century European engagement with Asian design. Nearby Canton Village included manufacturing buildings and court living quarters.

sectionTitles: Seafaring and the journeys of objects

passages.text: Taíno describes diverse late precolonial Caribbean societies, especially in the Greater Antilles, rather than every population that previously lived on the islands. Their communities combined farming, ceremonial gatherings and connections maintained through travel across the sea.

passages.title: Food and household materials
passages.text: Starch analysis of clay griddles reveals different foods at neighbouring sites. El Flaco in the Dominican Republic yielded evidence especially of maize; La Luperona of zamia; and Palmetto Junction in the Turks and Caicos Islands of manioc. These are findings from sampled tools, not complete menus.

passages.title: Food and household materials
passages.text: A clay griddle’s shape does not prove that it cooked only cassava bread. Microscopic residues reveal a wider range of plant preparation. Some surfaces may also have served for processing without heating, so researchers compare plant traces, damage and archaeological context.

passages.title: Food and household materials
passages.text: The Smithsonian describes bohío houses made with local materials such as palms and vines. Its conuco examples show family gardens as working spaces whose crops changed after plants arrived from other continents.

passages.title: Food and household materials
passages.text: Dried calabash gourds became bowls, spoons, containers and maracas. One plant supplied household utensils and musical instruments, joining practical work with performance.

passages.title: Games, performance and skilled carving
passages.text: Ceremonial plazas hosted batey, a team game played with a rubber ball. These substantial communal spaces also supported ritual gatherings. Their central position shows that organised recreation and public life mattered alongside subsistence work.

passages.title: Games, performance and skilled carving
passages.text: Areytos brought together storytelling, song, dance and drumming. Their forms varied with occasions such as celebrations, deaths or conflict. They carried collective knowledge through performance rather than following one uniform programme on every island.

passages.title: Games, performance and skilled carving
passages.text: A British Museum duho, or ritual seat, was carved from dense guayacan wood as a crouching human figure. Geometric patterns mark its back. The object combines furniture, bodily imagery and close attention to a difficult, durable material.

passages.title: Games, performance and skilled carving
passages.text: Gold inlays accent the duho’s eyes, mouth and shoulders. The museum interprets these features through chiefs’ and ritual specialists’ relationships with ancestor spirits. Its radiocarbon range, 1292 to 1399, concerns the wood; it cannot identify an exact day or year of carving.

passages.title: Seafaring and the journeys of objects
passages.text: Canoes carried people and goods between islands. Colonial accounts describe arrivals from other islands for exchange, while decorated vessels could also express status. Maritime knowledge made water a route of social connection as well as a demanding physical environment.

passages.title: Seafaring and the journeys of objects
passages.text: Another duho, from Eleuthera in the Bahamas, has an inscription recording that James Thompson found it while enslaved around 1820. He was free when he sold it to a missionary in 1835. Its later collection history adds another colonial story to the older object.

passages.title: Knowledge carried forward
passages.text: The Smithsonian guide pictures Leonarda “Doña Esmeralda” Morales-Acevedo stripping maguey fibre for hammock thread in Puerto Rico. This named maker’s work documents living craft knowledge, while contemporary Taíno cultural movements challenge accounts that declare all Caribbean Native people extinct.

Spanish colonization killed, displaced and enslaved Native people and undermined their political and religious institutions. Survivors carried knowledge into changing Caribbean communities. Contemporary Taíno identities and cultural renewal make an extinction ending inaccurate, even while the scale of colonial destruction must remain clear.

passages.text: The Tang dynasty is considered China's golden age, marked by cosmopolitan culture, Buddhist flourishing, poetic achievement and international trade. Chang'an became one of the world's largest cities, connected by the Silk Road to Central Asia, India and Persia.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: The Diamond Sutra, the world's oldest dated printed book, produced using woodblock printing.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: The first written warning of gunpowder's power appears in a Daoist alchemical text, describing a mixture of saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal that burst into flame.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The great poets Li Bai, Du Fu and Wang Wei create masterpieces of Chinese verse.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Buddhist cave temples at Dunhuang filled with murals and sculptures.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: True porcelain, the white Xing wares of Hebei, is made, though it remained rare and precious.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The monk Xuanzang travels to India, returning in 645 with Buddhist texts that he translates.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Christianity arrives in Chang'an with the missionary Alopen; the Xi'an Stele of 781 records its reception.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Chang'an reaches a population of about one million, with foreign merchants, monks and diplomats.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Tea drinking becomes widespread; Lu Yu writes the Classic of Tea.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Silk Road trade connects China to Central Asia, Persia and the Mediterranean.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Tang poetry became the standard for later Chinese literature.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Overseas Chinese still call a Chinatown a Tangrenjie, the street of the Tang people.
The An Lushan Rebellion of 755 fatally weakened the dynasty; regional military governors gained power, and the last Tang emperor was deposed by Zhu Wen in 907.

passages.text: Teotihuacan was a major urban center in central Mexico. Its public monuments, apartment compounds and specialized arts connected a large city with other Mesoamerican communities through exchange and influence.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The urban layout incorporated the San Juan River, whose course was altered to cross the Avenue of the Dead.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: Builders used talud-tablero profiles, combining sloping and upright wall sections, in civil and religious architecture.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Apartment compounds grouped connected rooms around open courtyards. They provided durable shared housing for much of the city's population.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Murals decorated many buildings, especially residential compounds. Artists also made mold-pressed ceramics and geometric stone faces.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Imported craft goods included worked obsidian and Thin Orange pottery. Stackable bowls made long-distance transport more practical.

passages.title: Change over time
passages.text: The Met's updated account places burning in the monumental core around 550 CE and marked population decline after 600. The people responsible are unidentified.

passages.text: The Tibetan Empire rose under Songtsen Gampo in the seventh century and for two hundred years matched Tang China and the Arab caliphate for control of the Silk Road, from the Tarim Basin to the Himalaya. It gave Tibet its script, its first monasteries and its Buddhism.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Songtsen Gampo married Princess Wencheng of Tang, who brought a Buddha image and texts to Lhasa; a Nepalese princess, Bhrikuti, is remembered as his other Buddhist queen.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Tibetan script was created, by tradition by Thonmi Sambhota, from an Indian script of the Gupta type.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Samye, the first Tibetan Buddhist monastery, was completed under Trisong Detsen, and Buddhism spread beside the native Bon rites.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Jokhang temple was built in Lhasa and became Tibet's holiest shrine.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Tibetan armies fielded armored cavalry and took fortified towns with methods learned from China and Central Asia.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Tibet held the Tarim oases and, from 786 to 848, Dunhuang, taxing the Silk Road between China, India and Central Asia.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: A Tibetan army occupied the Tang capital Chang'an for about two weeks.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: A peace treaty with Tang was carved in Tibetan and Chinese on a pillar that still stands outside the Jokhang.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Tibetan script is in use today across Tibet, Bhutan and the Himalaya.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Buddhism became the core of Tibetan identity and culture.
The emperor Langdarma was assassinated in 842 and the empire broke into rival kingdoms, the Era of Fragmentation, that lasted until the eleventh century.

passages.text: Tula in central Mexico was a major city of craftspeople, traders and monumental builders. Its political reach remains debated: connections through objects and stories do not by themselves establish the borders of a Toltec empire.

passages.title: Making tools and moving goods
passages.text: An excavated obsidian workshop combined residential compounds, refuse dumps and probable outdoor working spaces. Microscopic fragments in soil helped identify places where stone was worked. Production took place within a lived environment, not only inside monumental buildings.

passages.title: Making tools and moving goods
passages.text: The workshop received large, roughly prepared obsidian cores from more than one source. Craftspeople reduced them into cores for narrow blades, blades themselves and further blade products. The discarded pieces preserve stages of this skilled manufacturing sequence.

passages.title: Making tools and moving goods
passages.text: Tohil plumbate vessels at Tula connect the city with pottery production in Chiapas and Guatemala. Tracing where ceramics were made reveals routes of exchange; finding a foreign vessel does not show that its makers were governed from Tula.

passages.title: Making tools and moving goods
passages.text: Potters used multiple brushes together to paint repeated lines, and moulds helped produce vessels efficiently. Excavated moulds turn a proposed manufacturing technique into a directly documented practice.

passages.title: Cooking, gathering and shared space
passages.text: At rural Tepetitlán, hearths and cooking vessels identify areas where meals were prepared and eaten. A patio also contained an altar and other activity remains, suggesting that ordinary work and shared ritual occupied connected domestic spaces.

passages.title: Cooking, gathering and shared space
passages.text: Tepetitlán yielded many cooking pots but few fragments of the usual griddle type. The researcher offered alternative explanations, including use of other vessels. Archaeology cannot turn this small sample into certainty that residents did, or did not, make tortillas.

passages.title: Cooking, gathering and shared space
passages.text: Carbonised maize stems and roots at Tepetitlán provide evidence for cultivation and burning harvested fields. Other remains include amaranth and wild plants such as prickly pear and mesquite. Their survival helps reconstruct resources without supplying a complete household diet.

passages.title: Cooking, gathering and shared space
passages.text: The plant study also identified materials used as fuel, including thorny shrubs, yucca and prickly pear. Keeping a hearth burning required knowledge of the surrounding dry landscape, alongside the work of raising crops.

passages.title: Stone, colour and public architecture
passages.text: Human-shaped columns on Pyramid B once supported a temple roof. Carved equipment includes spearthrowers and butterfly-shaped breastplates, while surviving pigment shows that the figures were coloured. Structure and representation worked together.

passages.title: Stone, colour and public architecture
passages.text: A clay warrior wearing a jaguar helmet was fired and inlaid with mother-of-pearl. Pohl connects its shell material with the Gulf of California. The object combines modelling, firing and inlay with access to distant materials.

passages.title: Stone, colour and public architecture
passages.text: Reclining sculptures known as chacmools turn their heads sideways and support a receptacle on the abdomen. Tula’s architectural friezes also feature jaguars, coyotes, eagles and feathered serpents, placing powerful imagery within public ceremonial settings.

passages.title: Stone, colour and public architecture
passages.text: Housing varied in scale, construction and location. The museum describes groups of rooms arranged around shared patios, where domestic and ritual activities could take place. The city’s inhabitants did not all live in one standard kind of house.

The Tollan city was abandoned and monumental buildings burned, but these were not necessarily one event. The 2021 study leaves the destroyers unidentified. Later visitors and settlers reused the ruins, so political collapse did not erase the place or its significance.

passages.text: Tonga's modern kingdom combines a continuing monarchy and parliamentary institutions with vigorous traditions of textile work, poetry, language and community exchange. Surviving barkcloth can record particular events and reveal how makers worked. Political changes in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries reshaped government without ending Tongan cultural life.

passages.title: Objects that remember events
passages.text: A 1940s ngatu hingoa at Te Papa depicts a Spitfire seen from below. It commemorates Tongan support for the Allied war effort. Its makers are unnamed in the surviving collection history, so the detailed design should not be assigned to an invented individual artist.

passages.title: Objects that remember events
passages.text: Conservation examination of that cloth identified two layers of beaten mulberry bark, joined unevenly. The proposed starch adhesive and plant dyes remain qualified identifications. Damage, joins and repairs allow the cloth to be studied as a made object as well as an image.

passages.title: Objects that remember events
passages.text: Another large ngatu was made for Elizabeth II's visit in 1953 and later placed beneath Queen Salote's coffin on her return to Tonga in 1965. Its changing ceremonial use gives one textile a history spanning celebration and mourning.

passages.title: Making, measuring and exchanging cloth
passages.text: In a koka'anga work party, women join sheets of beaten inner bark in overlapping layers. They rub dye over cloth laid above kupesi pattern boards, bringing the designs through the surface, then add details by hand. The technique combines repeated patterns with individual decisions.

passages.title: Making, measuring and exchanging cloth
passages.text: Lines and numbers at the cloth's border mark langanga, units used to measure its growing length. Te Papa explains that the unit varies with the equipment and the maker. The markings record practical production knowledge, rather than a universal fixed metric.

passages.title: Making, measuring and exchanging cloth
passages.text: Ngatu circulate as gifts at weddings, funerals and other gatherings. Exchanges with makers of pandanus mats connect communities with different plant resources. Cloth therefore participates in relationships as well as furnishing and dress.

passages.title: Ideas and political institutions
passages.text: The first parliament opened on 16 September 1875 to discuss the new constitution. Its members included ministers, nobles and elected representatives. This opening date records an institutional event; it is not the day Tongan people or their islands began to have a history.

passages.title: Ideas and political institutions
passages.text: Charles St Julian sent George Tupou I a copy of Hawaii's 1852 constitution. Tonga's parliamentary history identifies it as an influence on the new constitutional text. This is a documented Pacific connection in political ideas, not evidence that the two systems were identical.

passages.title: Ideas and political institutions
passages.text: The original parliament could debate taxation and public spending and make laws, while questions such as succession to the throne remained outside its authority. These distinctions show how representation developed within a monarchy.

passages.title: Language, creativity and community life
passages.text: Queen Salote contributed poetry and songs to Tongan cultural life. Her work used the Tongan language creatively, making the history of monarchy also a history of composition and performance.

passages.title: Language, creativity and community life
passages.text: Tongan migrants in New Zealand first held language-specific church gatherings in private homes and later established larger congregations. Since the 1980s, community preschools have helped children learn Tongan. These institutions support language through regular shared activity.

passages.title: Language, creativity and community life
passages.text: Czarina Wilson's Tonga-flag face mask, made in May 2020, entered Te Papa's collection. It records a designer applying her skills to a new public-health need. Contemporary objects like this keep the cultural story open beyond historical monuments and royal occasions.

The British protectorate ended in 1970, and Tonga joined the Commonwealth that year. The kingdom continues. Its constitution, community institutions, language and artistic practices have changed across generations rather than ending at the map's last recorded snapshot.

passages.text: Totonac histories belong to the varied coastal and mountain landscapes of Veracruz and Puebla. Cities and communities shared some practices with neighbours while retaining local differences. Cempoala provides a documented example of urban life, rather than a model for every Totonac settlement.

passages.title: Water, cultivation and city design
passages.text: Cempoala’s production areas lay both within and beyond its dispersed urban settlement. Cultivation and residence were interwoven, so the city should not be imagined as a compact block of buildings surrounded by all of its fields.

passages.title: Water, cultivation and city design
passages.text: INAH describes walls protecting Cempoala against floods, channels bringing river water into the city and drains carrying wastewater toward cultivation. Managing water involved supply, protection and disposal together.

passages.title: Water, cultivation and city design
passages.text: Cempoala’s temples included square and circular foundations. The circular building associated with Ehecatl contrasts with the square-based Quetzalcoatl temple, showing variation within one ceremonial centre.

passages.title: Water, cultivation and city design
passages.text: At Yohualichan, INAH interprets architectural niches as references to caves in the surrounding region. Niches also appear at other sites, including El Tajín. Shared forms reveal connections, but alone cannot demonstrate that all such places belonged to one political state.

passages.title: Food and textile skills
passages.text: INPI’s account of later Totonac cuisine describes maize, beans and many edible greens, along with foods such as bocoles and handmade tortillas. This is evidence of a living regional cuisine; its complete modern ingredient list should not be projected into preconquest kitchens.

passages.title: Food and textile skills
passages.text: Backstrap weaving produces garments and household cloths. INPI describes Papantla makers using cotton or acrylic thread for a raised, soft-textured finish called confitillo. The presence of newer fibres shows a craft tradition adapting its materials.

passages.title: Performance and shared knowledge
passages.text: In the Voladores ceremony, four performers descend on ropes from a tall pole while the caporal plays a flute and small drum above them. The coordinated movement, music and height make the ceremony a demanding collective performance.

passages.title: Performance and shared knowledge
passages.text: UNESCO describes the ceremony as expressing relationships with nature and spiritual powers, including the sun and winds. It is especially associated with Totonac communities but also practised by other peoples. One community’s version should not stand for every performance.

passages.title: Performance and shared knowledge
passages.text: The Centre for Indigenous Arts organises learning through houses devoted to pottery, textiles, music, cuisine and other arts. Elders teach values alongside technique. Totonac language is a medium of instruction, making cultural transmission part of everyday educational practice.

passages.title: Performance and shared knowledge
passages.text: The centre’s safeguarding work includes recovering techniques and restoring plants and trees needed for artistic practice. This links the future of crafts with their material environments, as well as with the teachers and apprentices who keep knowledge in use.

Alliance against the Mexica did not preserve independence from Spain. Colonial rule imposed labour and religious demands and later reorganised local authorities. Totonac communities continued, adapting institutions and maintaining languages and creative traditions; no single city’s decline ends their history.

sectionTitles: Monuments and the evidence for power
Changing institutions and a living legacy

passages.text: The Tu'i Tonga chiefly line was associated with monumental centers on Tongatapu and far-reaching Pacific relationships. Excavated stone tools, royal tombs and collected household objects reveal different aspects of this history. Sacred chiefly rank, practical government and overseas exchange changed over time; they should not be compressed into a single unchanging empire.

passages.title: Monuments and the evidence for power
passages.text: At Heketa in eastern Tongatapu, fieldwork recorded house and seat platforms, a tiered tomb and the Ha'amonga trilithon. Their arrangement joined domestic, ceremonial and chiefly spaces. Clark and Reepmeyer interpret this complex as part of a new political order taking shape in the fourteenth century.

passages.title: Monuments and the evidence for power
passages.text: Ha'amonga is built from two upright coral-limestone slabs supporting a third slab across the top. Tonga's heritage submission links it to Tu'itatui through oral tradition. The monument demonstrates large-stone construction; a proposed astronomical purpose is less securely established.

passages.title: Monuments and the evidence for power
passages.text: The langi at Lapaha are raised burial platforms faced with carefully fitted stone. Moving, shaping and placing those blocks required coordinated labor. The structures preserve evidence of chiefly funerary practice, while continued care connects them with living communities.

passages.title: Voyaging, tools and exchange
passages.text: A 2014 study compared the chemistry of stone tools from Tongan chiefly centers with Pacific stone sources. Many pieces came from Samoa or Fiji, and one adze was traced to the Society Islands. The findings show material moving over long sea routes.

passages.title: Voyaging, tools and exchange
passages.text: In that study, 29 of 44 analyzed adzes and flakes from the state-period sample were nonlocal. The authors interpret the concentration of imports at chiefly centers as evidence of intensified exchange and political connections. Imported stone alone does not establish conquest of its source island.

passages.title: Households and skilled work
passages.text: A wooden kali in the Cook-Forster collection has a narrow head support carried on curved legs. Eighteenth-century observers described Tongans using these objects while sleeping. This household object shows careful woodworking directed toward an ordinary bodily need.

passages.title: Households and skilled work
passages.text: A food hook in the Pitt Rivers Museum retains an original wooden disk painted with bird figures. The hook attached to it is a later replacement. Reading that repair history matters: the whole object on display cannot be treated as untouched evidence from the collecting voyage.

passages.title: Households and skilled work
passages.text: Te Papa's account of eighteenth-century Tonga describes ngatu barkcloth used for bedding and clothing as well as other everyday purposes. Making useful cloth from inner bark connected plant cultivation, beating, joining and decoration with household life.

passages.title: Households and skilled work
passages.text: Clark and Reepmeyer connect Heketa's ceremonial spaces with kava drinking and presentation of first fruits to chiefs. In their interpretation, cultivated food and formal gatherings helped express the sacred standing of the Tu'i Tonga.

passages.title: Changing institutions and a living legacy
passages.text: The Tu'i Ha'atakalaua and Tu'i Kanokupolu lines exercised governing authority as the Tu'i Tonga retained sacred rank. Their relationships developed through succession, marriage and conflict. A list of Tu'i Tonga titleholders is therefore not a complete list of rulers exercising the same powers.

passages.title: Changing institutions and a living legacy
passages.text: Laufilitonga, the last Tu'i Tonga titleholder, died in 1865. George Tupou I's constitutional government followed in 1875, but the earlier transfer of power was a process rather than a single foreign conquest.

passages.title: Changing institutions and a living legacy
passages.text: At Lapaha, community leaders and researchers have worked together to repair stone structures and train residents in conservation. The tombs remain places of cultural responsibility, with archaeological research contributing to their protection.

The Tu'i Tonga title ended with Laufilitonga's death in 1865, after governing power had already shifted among chiefly lines. Tonga developed a constitutional monarchy under George Tupou I in 1875. Tongan communities and their heritage continued; neither date marks their disappearance.

passages.text: Vanuatu brings together island communities with distinct languages, histories and customary institutions. Lapita pottery, food remains, chiefly places and sand drawings reveal settlement, skilled work and ways of remembering. The republic became independent in 1980; the peoples and cultural practices of its islands have much longer histories.

passages.title: Discoveries at Teouma
passages.text: Quarrying at Teouma on Efate exposed a Lapita site in 2003. Archaeologists recovered decorated pottery and a cemetery, bringing evidence of skilled ceramic production together with burial practices. These finds concern early settlement of the islands, long before the modern state.

passages.title: Discoveries at Teouma
passages.text: A 2014 study analyzed stable isotopes in bone collagen from Teouma and compared them with animal and plant samples. The results point to dietary protein from reef and other marine foods, wild land animals and domestic animals. This evidence does not describe every ingredient of a meal.

passages.title: Discoveries at Teouma
passages.text: The researchers interpreted pig and chicken isotope values as consistent with animals feeding freely around the settlement. They also identified possible differences in access to protein. These are hypotheses about husbandry and food distribution, not direct observations of a household's daily routine.

passages.title: Chiefly places and remembered history
passages.text: Chief Roi Mata's Domain connects a residence on Efate, a place of death on Lelepa and a burial site on Artok. UNESCO dates the associated final chief to the early seventeenth century. Archaeology and oral traditions inform the interpretation of these connected places.

passages.title: Chiefly places and remembered history
passages.text: Customary tabu restrictions around Roi Mata's residence and burial place have shaped land use for centuries. Their continued observance makes the landscape part of living authority and memory, rather than only a collection of abandoned remains.

passages.title: Sand drawing, learning and communication
passages.text: In central and northern Vanuatu, a drawer can trace a continuous line across an imagined grid in sand, ash or clay. The resulting design can carry a story, message or body of knowledge. Mastery involves both controlling the line and explaining its significance.

passages.title: Sand drawing, learning and communication
passages.text: Sand drawings help people remember histories, kinship, songs, farming techniques and craft designs. A pattern can have several meanings in different settings. Presenting it merely as decoration leaves out the relationships between the drawing, its performer and its listeners.

passages.title: Food and shared work
passages.text: Laplap combines grated root crops with coconut cream, wrapped in leaves and cooked with heated stones. Contemporary versions use ingredients such as taro, yam or cassava. The preparation brings gardening, grating, wrapping and control of heat into a meal shared at gatherings or sold in markets.

passages.title: Food and shared work
passages.text: Simboro wraps grated plant foods in leaves and cooks them in coconut cream. The dish shows how leaves serve as cooking material as well as food. Recipes and ingredients vary, so a present-day description should not be projected unchanged into the Lapita period.

passages.title: Independence and cultural research
passages.text: The joint British and French colonial system ended when Vanuatu gained independence on 30 July 1980. Political independence concerned the authority of the state; it did not create the island communities or the customary relationships that had sustained them.

passages.title: Independence and cultural research
passages.text: The Vanuatu Cultural Centre's fieldworker network brings community researchers into documentation and teaching. Its 2018 film used interviews and archival material to explain how men and women record knowledge and support cultural renewal in their own communities.

Colonial joint administration ended in 1980, and Vanuatu continues as an independent republic. Island communities maintain and adapt languages, chiefly relationships, food practices and art. The passing of an individual chief or a colonial regime is distinct from the continuation of the people.

passages.text: Venice joined lagoon engineering to a far-reaching artistic culture. This chapter follows the city and its painters during the Renaissance; it does not yet cover the republic's entire history.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: During the republic, canals connected settlements consolidated from lagoon islands. Hydraulic and architectural work continually reshaped the relationship between the city and its surrounding water.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: In sixteenth-century Venice, Titian, Veronese and Tintoretto developed influential approaches to painting. Their work later shaped artists including Rubens and Velazquez.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: After moving from Verona in the 1550s, Veronese found both civic and church commissions in Venice. Artistic employment crossed religious and governmental settings.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The lagoon included fishing settlements and artisan communities such as Murano. Venice's palaces were part of a larger landscape of work and settlement.

passages.text: Vijayanagara, founded on the Tungabhadra in 1336, ruled the south of India for three centuries and made its capital, today's Hampi, one of the largest cities in the world. It kept the temple culture of the Tamil and Kannada country alive and traded horses and spices with the Portuguese, the Arabs and China.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Gopurams, towered gateways, and pillared halls carried Dravidian temple building to its most elaborate.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Under Krishnadevaraya (1509 to 1529) the Krishna temple was built at Hampi and the Vittala temple gained its stone chariot and musical pillars.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Krishnadevaraya kept eight Telugu poets at court and wrote the Amuktamalyada himself; Kannada, Tamil and Sanskrit letters flourished too.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Arab and Portuguese traders sold the warhorses the empire needed; Hampi's markets sold diamonds, spices and cloth.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The Portuguese Domingo Paes, who saw the city about 1520, called it as large as Rome and the best provided city in the world.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Estimates of the capital's people run to several hundred thousand, among the largest cities of the sixteenth century.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Canals from the Tungabhadra and large tanks watered the fields around the city.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Group of Monuments at Hampi was listed by UNESCO; more than 1,600 remains survive.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The empire's temple styles and its Nayaka successors kept Hindu kingship alive in the south.

The Deccan sultanates crushed the imperial army at Talikota in 1565 and sacked the capital. The Aravidu kings ruled a shrinking realm from Penukonda, Chandragiri and Vellore until Bijapur and Golconda took the last of it in 1646.

sectionTitles: Homes and skilled work at Reccopolis

passages.text: Visigothic royal power had an earlier centre at Toulouse and a later Iberian kingdom associated with Toledo. This card concentrates on the later kingdom, where excavated workshops and houses complement royal gifts, law and Latin scholarship. These different records show inventive adaptation of inherited traditions, but also inequalities and coercion within society.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work at Reccopolis
passages.text: Large houses in the early Visigothic city had circulation spaces leading to rooms, cooking areas and stables. Some were divided and enclosed during the seventh century. Changing walls and multiplying kitchens reveal households adapting existing buildings, rather than a town frozen in its founding plan.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work at Reccopolis
passages.text: Beside Reccopolis's main street, shops opened toward customers while workshops, stores and living spaces extended behind them. A circular glass furnace and associated processing structures survive. These remains place skilled production inside the town, close to both commercial activity and the palace approach.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work at Reccopolis
passages.text: The eastern craft building contained moulds for earrings and rings, balance pans and metalworking waste. Together these objects identify making and weighing, not merely possession of finished jewellery. They show the tools and discarded material behind the ornaments that survive in museum collections.

passages.title: Water engineering and its limits
passages.text: Reccopolis received water through a masonry aqueduct with a channel lined in waterproof mortar containing crushed ceramic. Surveyed remains preserve Roman construction principles in a late sixth-century project. Parts of its route remain missing and are reconstructed through terrain analysis rather than direct excavation.

passages.title: Water engineering and its limits
passages.text: Researchers argue that the aqueduct supplied more than the royal complex, proposing public distribution within the town. The volume of water and the hilltop setting support this interpretation. A complete network of household pipes and public fountains has not been excavated.

passages.title: Water engineering and its limits
passages.text: A tiled drain carried water from the courtyard of house 16000 toward the street. Other small drains and concave street surfaces suggest open channels for rain and overflow. This evidence should not be enlarged into a claim that the city possessed a complete underground sewer network.

passages.title: Goldwork, gifts and survival
passages.text: The Guarrazar treasure includes gold crowns and crosses decorated with stones, pearls and cut crystal. Letters hanging from Recceswinth's crown identify its royal donor. These were offerings for religious settings; the suspended crown should not be imagined as the king's everyday headwear.

passages.title: Goldwork, gifts and survival
passages.text: Guarrazar goldsmiths combined pierced or embossed sheets with settings and chains; some smaller crowns used open latticework. The treasure was concealed and later dispersed after its nineteenth-century discovery. Concealment shows an effort to protect valuable objects, but does not by itself establish one precise historical emergency.

passages.title: Organising and preserving knowledge
passages.text: Isidore of Seville's Etymologies organised subjects from grammar and mathematics to farming, textiles and household equipment through explanations of words. This was a work of compilation and interpretation. Its account of a craft does not establish that Isidore invented it or personally observed every process.

passages.title: Organising and preserving knowledge
passages.text: A manuscript of the Etymologies held by the Real Academia Espanola dates to the twelfth century, centuries after Isidore wrote. Such copies demonstrate the work's continuing transmission. The age of a surviving manuscript must be kept separate from the age of the text it carries.

passages.title: Law and unequal religious life
passages.text: A declaration addressed to Recceswinth in 654 required Jewish converts at Toledo to renounce Sabbath observance, religious festivals and dietary distinctions. Its coercive setting matters: the document records demands on a community, not free evidence that its members welcomed those demands.

passages.title: Law and unequal religious life
passages.text: Erwig's law of 681 threatened Jews who delayed baptism for themselves, their families or enslaved people with physical punishment, exile and confiscation. Royal religious uniformity came at others' expense. A prescribed penalty shows what authorities demanded, not proof that enforcement was identical everywhere.

The Umayyad conquest began in 711 and displaced Visigothic royal government over several years. It did not remove the peninsula's whole population or immediately empty its towns. Reccopolis continued into the Islamic period before declining much later, and Isidore's work continued to be copied. The map endpoint of 800 is not the kingdom's fall date.

passages.text: Mapuche histories encompass autonomous communities, exchange and creative work across southern South America. Relations with neighbours changed over centuries. Colonial resistance and later dispossession belong to this history alongside farming, family knowledge and living artistic traditions.

passages.title: Families, land and local authority
passages.text: The lof organised related families. In the historical model described by the National Library, a longko led a local group with limited authority. Wider alliances could form during war without creating a ruler with permanent jurisdiction over every community.

passages.title: Families, land and local authority
passages.text: The same account describes local leaders allocating fields to families and reassigning plots while depleted ground recovered. Reserve land provided another resource. Access depended on social relationships as well as cultivation, and arrangements changed under later restrictions.

passages.title: Weaving knowledge into daily life
passages.text: Textile specialists Matilde Painemil and Cristina Manquepi contributed family histories and practical knowledge to the museum’s collection study. Their expertise connected the handling of old cloth with forms and meanings still understood by makers.

passages.title: Weaving knowledge into daily life
passages.text: The textiles discussed include makuñ mantles, headbands and chañuntuku, thick woven saddle coverings. These are distinct objects for dress and other uses, rather than interchangeable examples of a single decorative pattern.

passages.title: Weaving knowledge into daily life
passages.text: Painemil describes design as mental and creative work, sometimes connected with dreams. She also teaches classes and makes commissioned textiles. Her account presents weaving as a skilled livelihood and an ongoing artistic practice, not merely repetition of inherited designs.

passages.title: Silver, clay and sound
passages.text: Mapuche silverwork includes the linked breast ornament trapelakucha, earrings called chaway and fastening pins such as tüpu. Specialists Antonio Chihuaicura and Marco Pailamilla examined such pieces with the museum, bringing makers’ knowledge to the interpretation of their construction and use.

passages.title: Silver, clay and sound
passages.text: Following nineteenth-century dispossession, families sometimes exchanged silver objects for food. The museum links these losses to the formation of public and private collections. An ornament’s museum history can therefore record hardship as well as artistic skill.

passages.title: Silver, clay and sound
passages.text: The same account describes craft knowledge surviving within families and being renewed through workshops, new pieces and replicas. Studying an old silver ornament and making a new one can both contribute to this continuing practice.

passages.title: Silver, clay and sound
passages.text: Potter Celinda Huaiquil explains links between water, women’s knowledge and ceramic vessels. Duck-shaped ketru metawe can pour liquids, including muday in ceremonies. Her interpretation joins close observation of living creatures with the practical work of shaping clay.

passages.title: Silver, clay and sound
passages.text: José Cayuqueo makes ritual drums using laurel wood and goatskin. He and Hernán Marinao also describe wooden pifüllka instruments accompanying the drum and supporting a machi’s ceremony. These are named makers’ accounts of living musical practice.

passages.title: People tell their own histories
passages.text: Manuel Manquilef’s writing and Pascual Coña’s orally narrated life preserve Mapuche perspectives on historical change. Coña’s account was recorded by a missionary, so the circumstances of recording matter alongside the narrator’s knowledge.

Chilean and Argentine expansion dispossessed communities and restricted land and movement. Later migration brought many Mapuche people to cities. These transformations did not end Mapuche life: makers, teachers, families and organisations continue to sustain and reshape their cultures.

passages.text: Wadawurrung Country includes landscapes around Geelong, Ballarat and the surrounding coast and plains. Stone arrangements, fishing places, plant knowledge and living art illuminate a history much older than colonial settlement. Wadawurrung people continue to care for Country and sustain cultural life after dispossession and environmental disruption.

passages.title: Stone arrangements and careful interpretation
passages.text: Wurdi Youang is an egg-shaped arrangement of basalt stones near Little River. A published survey describes an east-west axis and prominent stones at the western end. Its construction date is unknown, so the surviving arrangement cannot support a precise founding date or an age-based world record.

passages.title: Stone arrangements and careful interpretation
passages.text: The 2012 study identified two sets of alignments toward solstice and equinox sunsets and tested whether they might arise by chance. The authors interpret deliberate astronomical orientation. That finding does not establish every purpose of the place or recover all the knowledge associated with it.

passages.title: Stone arrangements and careful interpretation
passages.text: A public cultural assessment records stone fish traps at Point Lillias in Corio Bay. Basalt lines in the tidal zone and oral history support their interpretation. One site also has later oyster-industry remains, so the report distinguishes Indigenous use from subsequent modification.

passages.title: Food, materials and everyday knowledge
passages.text: Murnong, or yam daisy, supplied edible tubers on the plains. Accounts assembled in the cultural assessment describe digging sticks used to harvest them, with tubers eaten raw or roasted. Grazing animals introduced during colonization damaged this food landscape.

passages.title: Food, materials and everyday knowledge
passages.text: River red gum bark furnished material for bowls and shields. Golden wattle gum served as food and an adhesive for making implements. The same landscape could supply meals, containers and the means to repair or join tools.

passages.title: Food, materials and everyday knowledge
passages.text: The Wadawurrung Country Plan identifies reeds and grasses as resources for flour, weaving and string, alongside tubers, lilies, ochre and wood. Its priorities connect the health of plants with the continuation of practical and cultural knowledge.

passages.title: Food, materials and everyday knowledge
passages.text: Waterways, wetlands and Sea Country form connected responsibilities in the plan. Fish, eels, birds, camping places and cultural sites matter together, rather than being separated into food resources on one side and culture on the other.

passages.title: Creative practice and continuing authority
passages.text: The community's artists directory includes Tammy Gilson's weaving and Jenna Oldaker's painting, digital art and cultural education. These named practices show people carrying knowledge through both established materials and newer media.

passages.title: Creative practice and continuing authority
passages.text: The corporation was founded on 12 October 1998. Its initial appointment as a Registered Aboriginal Party came on 21 May 2009, with further Country included in 2013. These dates document recognition of an organization's role, not the creation of Wadawurrung identity.

passages.title: Creative practice and continuing authority
passages.text: The Country Plan links language, stories, ceremony and family participation with the protection of places and species. Development, extraction and environmental change therefore affect both ecosystems and the settings where cultural knowledge is practiced.

Wadawurrung people continue. Colonization brought dispossession and major changes to food landscapes, including damage from introduced grazing animals. Community institutions, artists and Country planning sustain cultural responsibilities; the final year shown for a map snapshot is not an extinction date.
